lessons.plain: A variable is a named box that holds a value so your program can use it later. JavaScript gives you three ways to make one. The older way, var, is loose: the box exists across a whole function and can be peeked at before you have put anything in it, so you quietly get 'nothing' instead of an error. The newer let and const are stricter. They only exist inside the nearest pair of curly braces, and touching them too early raises a clear error. const also refuses to let you swap the box for a different value. Think of var as a sticky note that's already on the fridge before you write on it.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a program prints a variable on one line and only creates that variable with var on the next line, do you think JavaScript will crash, print the value, or print something else? Make a guess before reading on.
lessons.teach:
A variable declaration creates a name bound to a value. JavaScript has three keywords for this. var is function-scoped: scope means the region of code where a name can be used, and for var that region is the whole enclosing function (or the whole script), ignoring if-blocks and loops. let and const are block-scoped: they exist only inside the nearest curly braces. let can be reassigned later. const cannot be reassigned, though an object or array it points to can still have its contents changed.

Hoisting is the reason var is risky. Before running a scope, the JavaScript engine registers every declaration in it, as if moved to the top. A var name is registered and set to undefined, the special 'no value yet' value. let and const names are registered but left uninitialised. The stretch from the start of the block to the declaration line is called the temporal dead zone (TDZ), and reading the name there throws a ReferenceError.

Worked example. Line 1: console.log(a); line 2: var a = 5. Step one: the engine hoists a and sets it to undefined. Step two: line 1 runs and prints undefined. Step three: line 2 assigns 5. No error appears. Swap var for let: step one registers a in the TDZ, step two throws ReferenceError: Cannot access 'a' before initialization, and the program stops at the real bug.

Common mistake: declaring var i inside an if-block or for-loop and assuming it vanishes afterwards. It does not; it leaks into the whole function and can overwrite another i or keep a stale value.

In a running system, var turns ordering bugs into silent undefined values that travel onward, for example into a request or a saved record, far from their cause. let and const fail loudly at the right line. The practical rule is to default to const, use let only when the value must change, and avoid var.

questions.prompt: A warehouse script contains these lines. Line 1: let stock = 3; Line 2: { Line 3: console.log(stock); Line 4: let stock = 7; Line 5: }. Trace it. Step one: line 1 runs, and the outer name stock holds 3. Step two: entering the block at line 2, the engine hoists the block's own let stock. It registers a new inner stock that is uninitialised, so the block is now in that name's temporal dead zone (TDZ). Step three: line 3 runs. What happens at step three?
choices: It prints 3, because the inner stock does not exist yet, so the outer one is used
It throws ReferenceError, because stock inside the block refers to the inner name, which is still in its TDZ
It prints 7, because hoisting moves the whole line 4, including its value, to the top of the block
It prints undefined, because the hoisted inner stock starts as undefined
questions.why: Inside the block, the hoisted inner let stock hides the outer one, and reading it before line 4 falls in its temporal dead zone, so a ReferenceError is thrown.

questions.prompt: A team writes: Line 1: const parts = ['bolt']; Line 2: parts.push('nut'); Line 3: parts = ['washer']; Which statement about these lines is correct?
choices: Line 2 throws an error, because a const array cannot have items added to it
Both lines throw errors, because nothing about a const value can ever change
Line 2 works and line 3 throws an error, because const forbids reassigning the name but allows changing the array's contents
Both lines work, because const only applies to numbers and strings
questions.why: const blocks reassignment of the name, as in line 3, but the array it points to can still be changed, as in line 2.

questions.prompt: What does this function print when called? function countCrates() { var n = 'none'; for (var n = 0; n < 4; n++) {} console.log(n); }
choices: 'none', because the loop's n disappears after the loop ends
4, because var is function-scoped, so the loop's n is the same variable and overwrites the earlier value
3, because the last value used inside the loop was 3
A ReferenceError, because n is declared twice
questions.why: var ignores the loop block, so both declarations are one function-wide n. The loop leaves n at 4, which is the value it has when it stops.

questions.prompt: In a shipping service, a function runs: sendToPrinter(city); and then, on the next line, var city = 'Oslo'; What happens in the running system when this function is called?
choices: The label is printed with 'Oslo', because hoisting moves the assignment up as well
The label is sent with undefined and no error appears, so the bad value travels on silently
The script refuses to start because of a syntax error
It throws a ReferenceError at the sendToPrinter line, which points straight to the bug
questions.why: Hoisting registers var city as undefined before the function body runs. The call therefore quietly passes undefined onward instead of failing at the line where the bug is.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, why the team style guide says 'prefer const, then let, never var'. Include what hoisting does to each keyword, and name one limit of const that people often misunderstand.
lessons.modelAnswer: All three keywords create variables, but they differ in scope and in how hoisting treats them. var is scoped to the whole function, so a var declared inside an if-block or loop leaks out of it. Hoisting registers a var at the top of its function and sets it to undefined, so reading it before its declaration line silently gives undefined instead of an error. That bug can travel far before anyone notices. let and const are scoped to their block. They are hoisted too, but left uninitialised in the temporal dead zone, so an early read throws a ReferenceError right where the mistake is. const also blocks reassignment, which signals intent. Its limit is that it is not deep immutability: a const array can still be pushed to, or an object property changed. You just cannot point the name at a new value.
rubricPoints: var is function-scoped while let and const are block-scoped.
Hoisting sets a var to undefined, so an early read silently gives undefined.
let and const sit in the temporal dead zone and throw a ReferenceError if read early.
const prevents reassignment but does not freeze object or array contents.
Silent undefined values are harder to trace than loud errors, which is why var is avoided.

suggested.rationale: The unit's mastery goal is predicting the output of snippets, which is best practised by running small var/let/const programs in a JavaScript lab and checking each prediction.

lessons.plain: Every value in JavaScript has a type, which is the kind of thing it is: text, a number, true-or-false, and so on. The simplest values are called primitives. JavaScript has a built-in tool that tells you a value's type. It also has two ways to ask whether two values are equal. The loose way quietly converts values to a common type before comparing them. The strict way does not convert anything. Think of the loose check as a cashier who accepts a written IOU as if it were cash, and the strict check as one who wants real cash only. The loose way often gives surprising answers.
lessons.guessPrompt: Is the text "5" the same as the number 5? Guess whether JavaScript says yes when it compares them loosely, and whether it says yes when it compares them strictly.
lessons.teach:
A primitive is a basic value that is not an object and cannot be changed in place. JavaScript has seven primitive types. A string is text. A number covers whole numbers and decimals alike. A bigint is a whole number too large for number. A boolean is true or false. Undefined means a variable has no value yet. Null is a value deliberately set to "nothing". A symbol is a unique identifier. Everything else, such as arrays and functions, is an object.

The typeof operator returns a string that names a value's type. For example, typeof 42 gives "number" and typeof "hi" gives "string". It has two quirks. First, typeof null gives "object". This is an old bug that was kept so existing code would not break. Second, typeof applied to a function gives "function".

Type coercion means JavaScript automatically converts a value from one type to another. The loose equality operator, ==, converts both sides toward a common type before it compares them. The strict equality operator, ===, compares without converting anything, so values of different types are never equal.

Here is a worked example with "5" == 5. Step 1: the types differ, because one side is a string and the other is a number. Step 2: == converts the string "5" into the number 5. Step 3: it compares 5 with 5 and returns true. Now try "5" === 5. Step 1: the types differ. Step 2: === stops there and returns false. Loose equality gives other surprises too. 0 == "" is true, because the empty string converts to 0. null == undefined is also true, while null === undefined is false.

A common mistake is using == to check form input. Text typed into a form arrives as a string. If someone leaves the quantity box empty, the value is "", and "" == 0 is true. In a running system, a blank field would be silently treated as zero, and an order with no quantity could be submitted instead of showing an error. The safe habit is to use === by default and to convert values yourself, for example with Number(), when you really want a number.

questions.prompt: A bike-rental app stores the number of bikes left at a dock as the number 3. A request from the website sends the requested count as the text "3". The code checks stock === "3". Trace it. Step 1: the left side is a number and the right side is a string, so the types differ. Step 2: ???. Step 3: the check fails, so the app wrongly reports that the dock does not have the requested bikes. What is Step 2?
choices: === stops because the types differ and returns false without converting anything
=== converts the number 3 into the string "3" and returns true
=== throws an error because a number cannot be compared with a string
=== converts the string "3" into the number 3, compares 3 with 3, and returns true
questions.why: Strict equality never converts types, so values of different types are never equal and the result is false.

questions.prompt: A weather station app sets a variable named reading to null on purpose when a sensor is offline. What does typeof reading return?
choices: "object"
"undefined"
"null"
"number"
questions.why: typeof null returns "object" because of an old bug that was kept so existing code would not break.

questions.prompt: A gym's signup form has a "number of guests" box. A visitor leaves it blank, so the code receives the value "" (an empty string). The code then runs if (guests == 0) to decide whether to skip the guest-pass step. What happens?
choices: The comparison is true, because == converts the empty string to 0, so a blank box is silently treated as zero guests
The comparison is false, because a string is never equal to a number
The comparison throws an error, because the box is empty
The comparison is false, because the empty string is converted to undefined
questions.why: Loose equality converts "" to the number 0 before comparing, so "" == 0 is true and the blank field passes as zero.

questions.prompt: In a parking app, the variable spot has not been given a value yet, so it is undefined. Which statement about comparing it with null is correct?
choices: spot == null is false and spot === null is false
spot == null is false and spot === null is true
spot == null is true and spot === null is true
spot == null is true and spot === null is false
questions.why: Loose equality treats null and undefined as equal, but strict equality does not, because they are different types.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what the primitive types are, what typeof tells you, and why the team should prefer === over ==. Include one limit or quirk they should watch for.
lessons.modelAnswer: JavaScript has seven primitive types: string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, null and symbol. Anything else, like an array or a function, is an object. You can check a value's type with typeof, which returns a name such as "number" or "string". It has a limit, though: typeof null says "object" because of an old bug, so you can't rely on typeof to detect null. Compare with === null instead. The == operator coerces, meaning it converts both sides to a common type before comparing. That's why "5" == 5 and "" == 0 are both true. The === operator never converts, so different types are always unequal. I'd use === by default and convert values on purpose, for example with Number() on form input. Otherwise an empty text box could quietly count as zero and let bad data through.
rubricPoints: Names the primitive types and says that everything else is an object.
Explains that typeof returns a string naming the type.
Mentions the typeof null quirk or another typeof limit.
Defines coercion and says that == coerces while === does not.
Gives a concrete surprising example such as "5" == 5 or "" == 0.
Recommends === by default with explicit conversion and notes the risk to real data.

suggested.rationale: Predicting the results of typeof and of == versus === is best learned by running small snippets in a JavaScript lab and comparing your guesses with what actually comes back.

lessons.plain: An operator is a small symbol that does something to values, like + for adding or > for comparing. An expression is any bit of code that works out to a single value, such as 3 * 4 or age > 18. When one expression holds several operators, JavaScript needs a rule for which one goes first. That rule is called operator precedence. It works like the order-of-operations rule from school maths, where multiplying happens before adding. Knowing this ranking lets you predict what a line of code will produce instead of guessing.
lessons.guessPrompt: In JavaScript, what value do you think 2 + 3 * 4 produces: 20 or 14? Why?
lessons.teach:
An operator is a symbol that does work on values, which are called operands. For example, + adds, * multiplies, > compares, && means "and", and = assigns. An expression is any piece of code that produces a value, such as 7, x, or price * qty + tax. Operator precedence is the ranking that decides which operator runs first when several share one expression. Associativity is the tie-break rule that decides the order when operators have equal rank.

Why it works: the JavaScript engine reads the whole expression and arranges it into a tree before computing anything. Higher-precedence operators bind more tightly, so they sit deeper in the tree and are computed first. Roughly, from tightest to loosest, the order is: parentheses, unary operators like ! and unary minus, exponent **, then * / %, then + -, then comparisons < > <= >=, then equality == ===, then &&, then ||, then the ternary ? :, and last assignment =. Most operators are left-associative, so 10 - 4 - 3 means (10 - 4) - 3, which is 3. But ** and = are right-associative, so 2 ** 3 ** 2 means 2 ** 9, which is 512.

Worked example: let total = 2 + 3 * 4 ** 2 > 40 && true;
Step 1: ** binds tightest, so 4 ** 2 is 16.
Step 2: 3 * 16 is 48.
Step 3: 2 + 48 is 50.
Step 4: 50 > 40 is true.
Step 5: true && true is true.
Step 6: assignment runs last, so total holds true.

Common mistake: assuming code runs strictly left to right, which would make 2 + 3 * 4 equal 20 instead of 14. A related trap is writing !count > 0 to mean "count is not above zero". The ! runs first and turns count into true or false, and only then is that compared with 0. JavaScript also rejects -2 ** 2 as a syntax error rather than guess what you meant. You must write (-2) ** 2 or -(2 ** 2).

Consequence: precedence bugs rarely crash a program. They quietly compute a wrong discount or a wrong permission check, and that result ships. Parentheses cost nothing and make your intent obvious.

questions.prompt:
A warehouse script decides whether an order can ship. hasStock is true.

let canShip = 30 - 8 / 4 * 2 >= 25 && hasStock;

Step 1: / and * share the same rank and are left-associative, so 8 / 4 runs first and gives 2.
Step 2: ???
Step 3: 30 - 4 is 26.
Step 4: 26 >= 25 is true.
Step 5: true && hasStock is true && true, which is true.
Step 6: Assignment runs last, so canShip holds true.

Which choice is the missing Step 2?
choices: 4 * 2 is 8, because multiplication outranks division.
2 * 2 is 4, using the result of Step 1.
30 - 8 is 22, because the expression is read left to right.
4 * 2 is 8 first, so 8 / 8 is 1.
questions.why: * and / have equal rank and are left-associative, so the 2 from 8 / 4 is then multiplied by 2 to give 4, which matches the 30 - 4 in Step 3.

questions.prompt: A ticketing app computes 40 / 5 / 2. Both operators are the same, so which rule decides the order, and what is the result?
choices: Precedence. The second / outranks the first, so it is 40 / (5 / 2), which is 16.
Associativity. Division is right-associative, so it is 40 / (5 / 2), which is 16.
Precedence. Division outranks every other operator, so the answer is 20.
Associativity. Division is left-associative, so it is (40 / 5) / 2, which is 4.
questions.why: Associativity is the tie-break for operators of equal rank, and / is left-associative, so the left division runs first: 40 / 5 is 8, and 8 / 2 is 4.

questions.prompt: A data-storage calculator contains the expression 2 ** 2 ** 3. What value does it produce?
choices: An error, because ** cannot be chained
questions.why: ** is right-associative, so it means 2 ** (2 ** 3), which is 2 ** 8, or 256. Grouping it as (2 ** 2) ** 3 would wrongly give 64.

questions.prompt: A library app wants to block borrowing when a member's loan count is not above 3. A developer writes the condition as !loans > 3. Why is this a bug?
choices: JavaScript rejects !loans > 3 as a syntax error, just like -2 ** 2.
The > runs first, so the code checks loans > 3 and then flips it, which is correct but slow.
The ! runs first on loans alone and turns it into true or false. Only that boolean is compared with 3. The intended check is !(loans > 3).
The && operator is needed instead of !, because ! only works on numbers.
questions.why: Unary ! has higher precedence than >, so it applies to loans before the comparison. Parentheses are needed to negate the whole comparison.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, how JavaScript decides the order in which operators in one expression run, using an example of your own. Name one situation where relying on precedence is risky and what you would do instead.
lessons.modelAnswer: An expression is code that boils down to one value, and operators are the symbols inside it that do the work. When several operators share an expression, JavaScript does not just go left to right. It uses precedence, a ranking where things like ** and * bind tighter than +, comparisons come after arithmetic, && comes before ||, and assignment happens last. When two operators have equal rank, associativity breaks the tie. Most go left to right, but ** and = go right to left. So 1 + 2 * 3 > 6 means 1 + 6 is 7, and 7 > 6 is true. The risk is mixed logic or unary operators. For example, !x > 0 negates x first, and -2 ** 2 is outright rejected. The tradeoff is that memorising the whole table is unrealistic and readers may misread it. So I add parentheses whenever the order matters, even if they are technically unnecessary.
rubricPoints: Defines an operator and an expression correctly.
States that precedence ranks operators and decides which runs first, not simple left-to-right order.
Mentions associativity as the tie-break for equal-rank operators, with ** or = as right-associative.
Traces a concrete example step by step to the correct result.
Names a risky case such as ! with comparison, mixed && and ||, or -2 ** 2.
Recommends explicit parentheses for clarity as the practical safeguard.

suggested.rationale: Predicting a value and then running real expressions in a JavaScript lab is the fastest way to make the precedence order stick.

lessons.plain: Conditional logic is how a program makes decisions: it checks whether something is true and picks which instructions to run. Think of a receptionist directing visitors. If you have an appointment, go upstairs; otherwise, wait here. JavaScript gives you three tools for this. The if/else statement handles general yes-or-no checks and chains of checks. The switch statement compares one value against a list of exact options, like a menu. The ternary operator is a compact one-line choice that hands back one of two values. Each tool fits a different shape of decision.
lessons.guessPrompt: A program checks a number. If it equals 200 it says "ok", if it equals 404 it says "missing", and otherwise it says "error". If the number is 404, which messages do you expect the program to produce, and why only those?
lessons.teach:
Conditional logic lets a program choose which code runs based on a condition. A condition is an expression that JavaScript treats as true or false. An if statement runs its block only when the condition is truthy, meaning it counts as true. An optional else block runs otherwise. An else if adds extra checks, tested top to bottom, and the chain stops at the first match. Falsy values count as false: 0, the empty string "", null, undefined and NaN. Almost everything else is truthy.

A switch statement compares one value against a list of case labels using strict equality, which requires the same type and the same value. Execution jumps to the matching case and keeps running downward until it reaches break, which exits the switch. A default label catches anything that matched no case. Switch reads well when one variable is checked against many fixed values.

The ternary operator, written condition ? a : b, is an expression, meaning it produces a value. It gives a if the condition is truthy and b otherwise. Use it for short either/or assignments, not for long logic.

Worked example with status set to 404. In if (status === 200) {...} else if (status === 404) {...} else {...}, the first test is false and the second is true. The 404 block runs and the else block is skipped. Now take switch (status) { case 200: msg = "ok"; break; case 404: msg = "missing"; case 500: msg = "error"; break; }. JavaScript jumps to case 404 and sets msg to "missing". That case has no break, so execution falls through into case 500 and sets msg to "error". The final value is "error".

Forgetting break is the common mistake. Fall-through raises no error. In a running system, a missing-page response could be logged as a server error and send engineers after the wrong problem. A related trap is that switching on the string "404" will not match case 404, because the comparison is strict.

Use if/else for ranges and mixed conditions, switch for one value against many exact matches, and the ternary for a single short choice that yields a value.

questions.prompt:
A bakery's checkout code sets a delivery fee from a customer's membership tier. The variable tier holds the number 2.

switch (tier) { case 1: fee = 10; break; case 2: fee = 5; case 3: fee = 0; break; default: fee = 20; }

Trace it step by step.
Step 1: JavaScript compares tier with case 1 using strict equality. 2 is not 1, so that case is skipped.
Step 2: tier matches case 2, so fee is set to 5.
Step 3: ???
Step 4: The break after case 3 is reached and execution exits the switch.
Final value of fee: 0.

Which choice correctly fills in Step 3?
choices: JavaScript throws an error because case 2 has no break, so fee is never finalised.
Because a matching case was found, execution exits the switch and fee stays at 5.
Because case 2 has no break, execution jumps to default and sets fee to 20.
Case 2 has no break, so execution falls through into case 3 and sets fee to 0.
questions.why: Without a break, a switch keeps running the code under the cases below the match, so case 3 runs and overwrites fee with 0 until its break exits.

choices: Nothing, because a ternary cannot produce a value
"in stock"
"sold out"
questions.why: 0 is falsy, so the ternary expression produces its second value, "sold out".

choices: "ground" and then "unknown", because of fall-through
"unknown"
An error is thrown because the types differ
"ground", because "7" and 7 look the same
questions.why: switch compares with strict equality, so the string "7" does not match the number 7 and the default label runs.

questions.prompt: A weather app must label a temperature as "freezing" below 0, "mild" from 0 up to 25, and "hot" above 25. Based on the guidance for choosing a conditional, which construct fits best?
choices: An if / else if / else chain, because the checks are ranges
A single ternary, because every result is a short string
A switch, because there are several possible labels to choose from
A switch with no break statements, so every label is considered
questions.why: if/else suits ranges and mixed conditions, while switch only matches one value against exact case labels.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide between if/else, switch, and the ternary operator for a piece of logic. Name one limit or trap of switch and one limit of the ternary.
lessons.modelAnswer: All three choose which code runs based on a condition, but they suit different shapes of decision. I use if/else when conditions differ in kind or involve ranges, like checking whether age >= 18 or whether a value is empty. The checks run top to bottom and stop at the first truthy one. I use switch when one value is compared against many exact options, like a status code. Its trap is fall-through: without break, execution keeps running into the next case, and nothing warns you. Switch also compares strictly, so the string "404" won't match the number 404. The ternary, condition ? a : b, is an expression that returns a value, so it's great for something like label = isAdmin ? "Admin" : "User". Its limit is readability: nesting ternaries or packing side effects into them makes the code hard to follow, so longer logic belongs in if/else.
rubricPoints: If/else runs the first branch whose condition is truthy and fits ranges or mixed conditions.
Switch matches one value against exact cases using strict equality.
Without break, a switch case falls through into the next case silently.
The ternary is an expression that returns one of two values.
Ternaries become hard to read when nested or used for long logic.

suggested.rationale: Running and modifying real if/else, switch, and ternary snippets in a JavaScript lab is the fastest way to see fall-through and truthiness behaviour for yourself.

lessons.plain: A loop tells the computer to repeat a chunk of work, either a set number of times or until something changes. JavaScript has several loop styles because there are different reasons to repeat. Think of a coffee shop. You can serve exactly ten customers by counting. You can keep serving while the queue is not empty. You can go through each person in the line. Or you can read the labels on every shelf. Choosing the style that matches your reason makes the code shorter, clearer and less likely to hide bugs.
lessons.guessPrompt: You have a list of three prices and want to add them up. Would you rather have a loop that hands you each price directly, or one that hands you each price's position number? Why might the second choice cause trouble?
lessons.teach:
A loop repeats a block of code called the body. Each pass through the body is an iteration. JavaScript has four common forms.

A for loop has three parts in its header. The first is a start step, such as let i = 0. The second is a condition checked before every pass, such as i < 3. The third is an update run after every pass, such as i++. Use it when you need a counter or an index, for example to step backwards or to skip every other item.

A while loop has only a condition, and it keeps running as long as that condition is true. Use it when you do not know the count in advance, such as retrying until a value arrives. If nothing in the body ever makes the condition false, you get an infinite loop that freezes the page or the server process.

A for...of loop walks through the values of an iterable. An iterable is anything that can hand out its items one at a time, such as an array, a string, a Map or a Set. Use it when you simply want each item.

A for...in loop walks through the enumerable property keys of an object. Enumerable keys are the property names marked as visible to looping, and they include keys inherited through the object's prototype. These keys always come out as strings. Use for...in to inspect an object's property names.

Here is a worked example. Start with const scores = [10, 20] and let total = 0.

With for (const s of scores) total += s, the first pass gives s = 10, so total becomes 10. The second pass gives s = 20, so total becomes 30.

Now swap in for (const k in scores) total += k. On the first pass, k is the string "0", and 0 + "0" produces the string "00". On the second pass, k is "1", and total becomes "001". The loop ran the right number of times, but it joined index names together instead of adding the values.

A common mistake is using for...in on arrays. Besides giving you string keys, it can pick up extra properties that someone added to the array or to its prototype. In a running system this causes silently wrong results rather than a visible error.

The rule of thumb is: use for...of for values, for...in for object keys, for when you need the index, and while when the stopping point is unknown.

questions.prompt: A bakery's display sign builds a word backwards. Start with const word = "pie" and let out = "". The loop is for (const ch of word) out = ch + out. Pass 1: for...of hands out the first character, so ch = "p" and out becomes "p". Pass 2: ch = "i", so out becomes "i" + "p", which is "ip". Pass 3: ch = "e", so out becomes ______. What value fills the blank?
choices: "pie"
"eip"
"ipe"
questions.why: for...of gives the string's actual characters, and putting "e" in front of "ip" produces "eip".

questions.prompt: A warehouse app must keep checking a delivery tracker until a "delivered" status shows up. Nobody knows how many checks that will take. Which loop form fits this best?
choices: while, because it keeps running as long as a condition is true and the count is unknown
for, because it always needs a fixed counter set in advance
for...in, because it walks through the tracker's property keys
for...of, because it hands out each item of an iterable
questions.why: A while loop suits work where the stopping point is unknown, such as repeating until a value arrives.

questions.prompt: A grocery tracker has const stock = { apples: 4, pears: 6 } and let n = 0. It runs for (const k in stock) n += k. What is n after the loop finishes?
choices: "applespears"
"0applespears"
questions.why: for...in gives the key names as strings, so 0 + "apples" becomes "0apples", and adding "pears" gives "0applespears".

questions.prompt: A server has let attempts = 0 and runs while (attempts < 3) { tryConnect(); }. Nothing inside the body ever changes attempts. What happens when this runs?
choices: It runs once and stops because tryConnect() was called
It throws a visible error on the fourth pass
It runs exactly three times and then stops
It loops forever because the condition never becomes false, which freezes the server process
questions.why: If nothing in the body ever makes a while condition false, the loop never ends, and an infinite loop freezes the page or server process.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you decide between for, while, for...of and for...in. Include one limit or tradeoff, such as what goes wrong when for...in is used on an array.
lessons.modelAnswer: I pick the loop based on what I actually need from each pass. If I just want each item of an array, string, Map or Set, I use for...of, because it hands me the values directly. If I need the position, for example to go backwards or compare neighbours, I use a classic for loop with a counter. If I don't know how many passes there will be, like retrying until something succeeds, I use while. With while, I have to make sure the body eventually makes the condition false, or the loop never ends. I save for...in for listing an object's property names. The tradeoff is that for...in gives keys as strings and can include inherited or extra properties. On an array, adding those keys concatenates strings instead of summing numbers, and you get a wrong answer with no error.
rubricPoints: for...of yields the values of an iterable such as an array, string, Map or Set.
for...in yields enumerable property keys as strings, including inherited ones, so it suits objects rather than arrays.
A classic for loop fits cases that need an index or counter control.
while fits an unknown number of repetitions, but risks an infinite loop if the condition never turns false.
Using for...in on an array can silently produce wrong results, such as string concatenation instead of a sum.

suggested.rationale: Running the same data through each loop form in a JavaScript lab and watching the outputs differ, such as "001" versus 30, builds the prediction skill this unit targets.

lessons.plain: A function is a reusable set of steps: you give it inputs, it does some work, and it may hand back a result. JavaScript offers three ways to write one. A declaration is like a recipe printed in a cookbook's index, available from the moment you open the book. An expression is like a recipe written on a card and dropped into a labelled box. You can only use it after the card is in the box. An arrow function is a shorter card format. It does not carry its own idea of who is doing the cooking. Instead, it borrows that from the place where it was written.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose you call a function on line 1, but the function itself isn't written until line 10. Will JavaScript run it, throw an error, or does that depend on how the function was written? Make a guess.
lessons.teach:
A function declaration is a statement that starts with the keyword function and a name, for example: function double(n) { return n * 2; }. Before any code runs, the engine scans the scope and registers every declaration. This is called hoisting. It means a declared function can be called on a line above where it appears.

A function expression creates a function as a value inside a larger expression, usually by assigning it to a variable: const double = function (n) { return n * 2; };. Only the variable is known in advance. With const or let, the variable cannot be read until its line has run, so an earlier call fails.

An arrow function is a shorter kind of expression: const double = (n) => n * 2;. If the body is a single expression, its value is returned automatically. Arrows also differ in behaviour. They have no this of their own, which is the object a function is acting on. Instead they reuse the this of the surrounding code. They also cannot be called with new to build objects.

Worked example, traced:
Step 1: the code console.log(a(3)); function a(n) { return n * 2; } prints 6. The engine registered a before running line 1.
Step 2: the code console.log(b(3)); const b = (n) => n * 2; throws a ReferenceError, "Cannot access 'b' before initialization". The name b exists, but it has no value yet.

A common mistake is writing an object method as an arrow: const counter = { count: 0, inc: () => { this.count++; } };. Inside the arrow, this is not counter. It is whatever this was outside the object, often undefined. Calling counter.inc() then either crashes or quietly updates the wrong thing, and count stays 0. A regular function or method shorthand, inc() { this.count++; }, binds this to counter when called as counter.inc().

The same borrowing behaviour helps elsewhere. An arrow used as a callback inside a method, for instance in setTimeout, keeps the method's this. That is exactly what you want there.

choices: It prints undefined, because tax exists but its value has not been set yet.
It throws a ReferenceError, because tax cannot be read until line 4 has run.
It prints 10, because only arrow functions fail when called before their line, and tax uses the function keyword.
It prints 10, because a function expression assigned to a variable is hoisted just like a declaration.
questions.why: Only the name tax is known in advance, and a const variable cannot be read before its line runs, so calling it on line 3 throws a ReferenceError.

questions.prompt: A music app has this object: const playlist = { plays: 0, play: () => { this.plays++; } };. After calling playlist.play(), the value of plays is still 0. Which change makes playlist.play() increase plays?
choices: Change const playlist to let playlist so the object can be updated.
Add a return statement, so the arrow becomes play: () => { return this.plays++; }.
Rewrite the method using method shorthand, play() { this.plays++; }, so that this is playlist when it is called as playlist.play().
Move the playlist object above every other line so that hoisting registers it first.
questions.why: An arrow has no this of its own and borrows the surrounding code's this, while a regular method called as playlist.play() gets playlist as this.

questions.prompt: A floor-planning tool defines const area = (w, h) => w * h;. What does area(5, 7) return?
choices: A ReferenceError, because arrow functions need curly braces around their body
undefined, because the arrow has no return keyword
35, because an arrow whose body is a single expression returns that expression's value automatically
NaN, because arrow functions cannot take two parameters without braces
questions.why: When an arrow's body is a single expression, the arrow returns that expression's value automatically, so 5 * 7 gives 35.

questions.prompt: A developer writes const Robot = (name) => { this.name = name; }; and then tries const r = new Robot("Bolt");. What is the result?
choices: It creates an object with no name property, because the arrow's this is the surrounding code's this.
It works only if Robot is declared before the line that uses new, because of hoisting.
It fails, because arrow functions cannot be called with new to build objects.
It creates an object whose name is "Bolt", the same as a function declaration would.
questions.why: Arrow functions cannot be called with new, so using one to build an object is an error.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between a function declaration, a function expression and an arrow function. Describe one concrete situation where choosing an arrow function would cause a bug, and one where it is the better choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: All three create functions, but they differ in when they exist and what this means inside them. A declaration, written as function name() {}, is hoisted, so you can call it before the line where it's written. A function expression is a function value assigned to a variable. With const it can't be called until that line runs, and an earlier call throws a ReferenceError. An arrow function is a compact expression. It has no this of its own and borrows this from the surrounding code. That is the tradeoff. If I write an object method as an arrow, like inc: () => this.count++, then this isn't the object, and the count never changes or the call crashes. But inside a method, if I pass a callback to setTimeout, an arrow keeps the method's this, while a regular function would lose it. Arrows also can't be used with new.
rubricPoints: Function declarations are hoisted and can be called before they appear in the code.
Function expressions assigned with const or let cannot be called before their line runs.
Arrow functions are a shorter expression syntax and can return a single expression implicitly.
Arrow functions have no own this; they take this from the surrounding code.
Using an arrow as an object method gives the wrong this, so the method breaks or misbehaves.
Arrows are a good fit for callbacks inside methods because they keep the outer this.

suggested.rationale: Running small snippets and watching hoisting errors and this-binding bugs happen is the fastest way to make these three forms stick, and the planned JavaScript lab would let the learner do that.

lessons.plain: When you write a function, you list names for the values it expects. These names are its parameters. Two features make those lists more flexible. A default value is a fallback the function uses when the caller leaves a value out. It works like a coffee order that comes with regular milk unless you ask for something else. A rest parameter is a catch-all that gathers any number of extra values into one list. It works like a basket that holds however many items the caller hands over. Together they let one function handle both short calls and long calls cleanly.
lessons.guessPrompt: A function is defined as function greet(name = "friend") { return "Hi " + name; }. What do you think greet() returns, and what do you think greet(null) returns? Are they the same?
lessons.teach:
A parameter is a named placeholder in a function's definition. An argument is the actual value passed in when the function is called. A default value is a fallback written in the parameter list, as in function greet(name = "friend"). JavaScript uses it only when the argument is missing or is exactly undefined, which is JavaScript's value for "nothing was given." A rest parameter is written with three dots, as in ...items. It collects every remaining argument into a real array, meaning an ordered list with tools such as length and reduce. It must be the last parameter, and a function can have only one.

Why it works: on each call, JavaScript matches arguments to parameters from left to right. Any parameter left without a value gets undefined, and a default replaces that undefined. Whatever arguments remain after the named parameters are filled go into the rest array. If none remain, the rest array is empty, never undefined.

Worked example: function total(taxRate = 0.2, ...prices) { return prices.reduce((sum, p) => sum + p, 0) * (1 + taxRate); }. Trace the call total(undefined, 10, 20). Step 1: taxRate receives undefined, so the default 0.2 is used. Step 2: the leftover arguments 10 and 20 become prices = [10, 20]. Step 3: reduce adds them to 30. Step 4: 30 × 1.2 = 36. Now call total(). This time prices is [], the sum is 0, and the result is 0.

Common mistake: expecting null, 0 or an empty string to trigger the default. They do not, because only undefined does. The call total(null, 10) sets taxRate to null. In arithmetic, null counts as 0, so the tax silently disappears. In a running system that produces a quietly wrong number rather than a crash, which is much harder to notice. Notice also that the example made callers pass undefined as a placeholder. That happens whenever a defaulted parameter sits before others, so place optional parameters as late as you can.

Rest parameters replace the older arguments object. That object is array-like but is not a real array, and it does not exist inside arrow functions.

questions.prompt:
A monitoring tool defines this function:

function logEvents(level = "info", ...messages) { return level + ": " + messages.length + " message(s)"; }

Trace the call logEvents("", "disk full", "retrying").

Step 1: ???
Step 2: The leftover arguments become messages = ["disk full", "retrying"].
Step 3: messages.length is 2.
Step 4: The function returns ": 2 message(s)".

Which statement correctly fills in Step 1?
choices: level receives undefined, because an empty string is treated as nothing being given.
The empty string is skipped and placed into messages, so level receives "info".
level receives "info", because an empty string counts as a missing argument and triggers the default.
level receives "", because only undefined triggers a default, and an empty string is not undefined.
questions.why: A default replaces only undefined, so the empty string is kept as level's value, which is why the result starts with ": " and has no "info".

questions.prompt: Which of these function definitions uses default values and rest parameters in a valid way?
choices: function report(title, ...rows, ...notes) { }
function report(...rows, title) { }
function report(...rows, title = "Summary") { }
function report(title = "Summary", ...rows) { }
questions.why: A rest parameter must be the last parameter and a function can have only one, and only this option follows both rules.

choices: NaN, because labels cannot be counted
questions.why: width is undefined so it uses the default 10, height is 0, which does not trigger the default, so 10 × 0 = 0, and labels holds three items, giving 0 + 3 = 3.

questions.prompt: A developer writes const countArgs = () => arguments.length; expecting countArgs("a", "b") to return 2, but it does not work. Which change fixes it?
choices: Rewrite it as (...args, extra) => args.length so the last value is kept separately.
Rewrite it as (...args) => args.length, because a rest parameter collects every argument into a real array.
Rewrite it as (args = []) => args.length so a missing list defaults to empty.
Leave it unchanged, because the arguments object works the same way in arrow functions.
questions.why: The arguments object does not exist inside arrow functions, but a rest parameter collects all the passed arguments into a real array that has a length.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how default values and rest parameters work in JavaScript, and name one limit or trap they should watch for when using them.
lessons.modelAnswer: Parameters are the named slots in a function definition, and arguments are the values a caller actually passes. A default value, like rate = 0.2, is a fallback. It applies only when the argument is missing or exactly undefined. Passing null, 0 or an empty string does not trigger it. That is the main trap, because null can slip through and quietly break a calculation instead of throwing an error. A rest parameter, written ...items, gathers all leftover arguments into a real array. If there are no leftovers, the array is empty, so you can call methods like reduce safely. It has to be the last parameter, and you only get one. A tradeoff: if a defaulted parameter comes before other parameters, callers must pass undefined as a placeholder. So keep optional parameters toward the end. Rest also replaces the old arguments object, which isn't a real array and isn't available in arrow functions.
rubricPoints: A default value is used only when the argument is missing or exactly undefined.
Passing null, 0 or an empty string does not trigger the default, which can cause silent wrong results.
A rest parameter collects remaining arguments into a real array that is empty if there are none.
A rest parameter must be last and there can be only one.
Defaulted parameters placed before others force callers to pass undefined as a placeholder.

suggested.rationale: Calling functions with missing, undefined, null and extra arguments and watching the results is the fastest way to internalise these rules, and the planned JavaScript lab would let learners do exactly that.

lessons.plain: Scope is the answer to one question: from where in my code can I see this name? Think of an office building. Some notes are pinned up for the whole floor, and others stay inside a single meeting room. In JavaScript, older-style variables are visible across the whole function, like the floor notice. Newer-style variables stay inside the nearest set of braces, like a note left in one room. The newer style also has a firm rule. The name exists from the moment you enter the room, but you may not read it until the line that creates it has run. Reading it any earlier stops the program with an error.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose you create a variable inside the curly braces of an if statement. Would you expect to be able to use it after the closing brace? Do you think it matters which keyword (var, let or const) you used to create it?
lessons.teach:
Scope is the region of code where a variable name can be seen and used. JavaScript has two kinds you meet daily.

Function scope means a variable is visible everywhere inside the function that declares it. The older keyword var works this way, and it ignores any curly braces in between. Block scope means a variable lives only inside the nearest pair of curly braces, such as an if body or a for loop. The keywords let and const work this way, and const also forbids reassigning the variable.

Why does this happen? Before running a block or function, JavaScript scans it and registers every declaration. This scan is called hoisting. A var is registered and immediately given the value undefined, so reading it early quietly returns undefined. A let or const is registered but left uninitialised until its declaring line runs. The stretch from the start of its scope to that line is the temporal dead zone (TDZ). Touching the name there throws a ReferenceError, which is the error JavaScript raises when a name cannot be used.

Worked example: function f() { console.log(a); console.log(b); var a = 1; let b = 2; }
Step 1: on entry, a is hoisted and set to undefined, while b is hoisted but uninitialised.
Step 2: console.log(a) prints undefined.
Step 3: console.log(b) runs inside b's TDZ, so it throws a ReferenceError and the function stops.

A second trace: if (true) { var x = 5; let y = 6; } Reading x after the closing brace gives 5, because var ignores the block. Reading y there throws a ReferenceError, because y existed only inside the block.

A common mistake is assuming var respects blocks. A var declared inside a loop body still exists after the loop, holding its last value. A later loop that reuses the name silently shares it.

In a running system, var bugs appear as wrong values with no error, which makes them slow to trace. TDZ bugs crash loudly, but only when that code path actually runs. That is why most teams default to const, use let when a value must change, and declare names before using them.

questions.prompt:
A shop's reporting code runs this function: function report() { console.log(count); var count = 3; if (count > 0) { let label = "ok"; } console.log(label); }
Step 1: On entry, count is hoisted and set to undefined. label belongs to the if block, so it is not visible at function level at all.
Step 2: console.log(count) prints undefined.
Step 3: count becomes 3, the if body runs, and label is created and set to "ok" inside that block only.
Step 4: ???
Which choice correctly completes Step 4?
choices: console.log(label) prints undefined, because label was hoisted to the function
console.log(label) prints undefined, because let acts like var after its block ends
console.log(label) prints "ok", because the if body already ran
console.log(label) throws a ReferenceError, because label existed only inside the if block
questions.why: let is block scoped, so once the if body's closing brace is passed the name label cannot be used, and reading it throws a ReferenceError.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes the temporal dead zone (TDZ)?
choices: The time between a var being hoisted and being assigned, during which it reads as undefined
The region outside any curly braces, where block-scoped variables are set to undefined
The stretch from the start of a let or const variable's scope to its declaring line, where using the name throws a ReferenceError
The part of a function after a return statement, where code never runs
questions.why: The TDZ applies to let and const: they are registered by hoisting but left uninitialised until their line runs, so touching them earlier throws a ReferenceError.

questions.prompt: A ticketing script contains: for (var seat = 0; seat < 3; seat++) { } console.log(seat); What does the last line do?
choices: Prints 2, the last value used inside the loop body
Prints 3
Prints undefined, because the loop has finished
Throws a ReferenceError, because seat belonged to the loop
questions.why: var ignores the loop's braces, so seat still exists after the loop and holds its last value, which is 3 after the final increment stops the loop.

questions.prompt: In a payroll service, a function reads a let variable named bonusRate on a line above where bonusRate is declared, but only inside a branch that runs for rare holiday payments. What is most likely to happen in the running system?
choices: Holiday payments quietly use undefined as the rate, giving wrong totals with no error
Normal runs are fine, but the code crashes with a ReferenceError when the holiday branch finally runs
The program refuses to start, because JavaScript rejects every early read during its scan
Nothing goes wrong, because hoisting moves the value of bonusRate to the top
questions.why: Reading a let inside its TDZ throws a ReferenceError, but only when that code path actually executes, so the bug stays hidden until a holiday payment triggers it.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks why the style guide bans var and wants let and const instead. In your own words, explain function scope versus block scope and what the temporal dead zone is. Name one tradeoff or limit of the TDZ rule, for example when its error actually shows up.
lessons.modelAnswer: var is function-scoped, so a var declared inside an if or a loop is still visible across the whole function. That makes it easy to overwrite or reuse a value by accident. let and const are block-scoped, so they only exist inside the nearest braces, which keeps names local to where they are needed. All three are hoisted, meaning JavaScript registers them before the code runs. But var starts as undefined, so reading it too early quietly gives a wrong value. let and const stay uninitialised until their line runs, and that window is the temporal dead zone. Reading the name there throws a ReferenceError. The tradeoff is that this error only appears when that exact code path executes, which might be rare or only happen in production. So the TDZ turns silent bugs into loud ones, but it does not catch them ahead of time. Declaring variables at the top of their block avoids it entirely.
rubricPoints: Defines scope as where a variable name can be seen and used.
States that var is function-scoped while let and const are block-scoped.
Explains hoisting: var starts as undefined, while let and const stay uninitialised.
Defines the temporal dead zone as the span before the declaration runs, where access throws a ReferenceError.
Names a limit, such as the TDZ error only appearing when that code path actually runs.

suggested.rationale: Predicting and then running small snippets that read variables before or outside their declarations is the fastest way to internalise scope and the TDZ, and the planned JavaScript lab would provide exactly that.

lessons.plain: A closure is what you get when a function remembers the variables that were around it when it was created, even after the surrounding code has finished running. Picture a worker leaving the office with a backpack. Inside are the notes from the room where they were hired, and those notes go wherever the worker goes. A closure is a live link to those variables, not a photocopy, so the worker can read them and change them later. Programmers use this to give a function its own private memory, such as a counter, a saved setting, or a cache that nothing else can touch.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose a function creates a variable called count set to 0 and then hands back a small inner function that adds 1 to count and returns it. The outer function has already finished. If you call the inner function three times, what do you expect it to return each time, and why?
lessons.teach:
A closure is a function together with the variables from the scope where it was defined. Scope means the region of code where a name is visible. In JavaScript, any function created inside another function can keep using the outer function's variables after that outer function has returned.

This works because a closure captures variables, not values. A variable here means the named storage slot itself, not the number or text it holds at one moment. The engine sees that an inner function still refers to that slot, so it keeps the slot alive instead of throwing it away when the outer function ends.

Here is a worked example. Take `function makeCounter() { let count = 0; return function () { count = count + 1; return count; }; }`. Run `const a = makeCounter();`. A fresh `count` is created with the value 0, and the inner function is returned and stored in `a`. `makeCounter` has now finished, but `count` survives because `a` refers to it. Calling `a()` raises `count` to 1 and returns 1. Calling `a()` again returns 2. Now run `const b = makeCounter();`. That call creates a brand-new `count`, so `b()` returns 1. The counters `a` and `b` never share state. No outside code can reach `count` directly, which makes it private.

Real uses follow the same pattern. A click handler can remember which item it belongs to. A function can be set up with a fixed setting, such as a tax rate, and reuse it on every call. A cache can store earlier results so they are not recomputed.

A common mistake is to think a closure takes a snapshot of the value. Consider `let greeting = 'hi'; const say = () => greeting; greeting = 'bye';`. Calling `say()` returns 'bye', because the closure reads the current contents of the slot.

In a running system, anything a closure refers to stays in memory for as long as the closure itself exists. A long-lived event handler that closes over a large array keeps that whole array alive, and this is a quiet source of memory growth.

choices: It finds free is 2 again, because free is reset to spaces on every call, so it returns 1.
It returns 'full', because makeGarage has already returned and free no longer exists.
It finds free is 1, lowers it to 0, and returns 0.
It finds free is 1 but cannot change it, because a closure only holds a read-only copy, so it returns 1.
questions.why: The closure keeps the same free variable alive between calls, so the second call sees the 1 left by the first call and lowers it to 0, which is why the third call then returns 'full'.

questions.prompt: A shipping company writes a function makeLabeler() that declares let nextNumber = 500 and returns an inner function that uses nextNumber. In plain terms, what does that inner function capture?
choices: Nothing, because nextNumber is discarded once makeLabeler returns
The variable nextNumber itself, the storage slot, which stays alive for the inner function
A copy of the whole makeLabeler function, which runs again on each call
A snapshot of the number 500, frozen at the moment makeLabeler ran
questions.why: A closure captures variables (the named storage slots), not values, and the engine keeps that slot alive because the inner function still refers to it.

questions.prompt: A gym's booking page has this code: let maxWeight = 50; const tooHeavy = (kg) => kg > maxWeight; maxWeight = 80; What does tooHeavy(60) return?
choices: undefined, because maxWeight was changed after the function was made
An error, because a closure cannot read a variable that has been reassigned
false, because the arrow function reads the current contents of maxWeight, which is now 80
true, because the arrow function remembered maxWeight as 50 when it was created
questions.why: The closure reads the variable slot at call time, so it compares 60 against 80, not against the earlier value 50.

questions.prompt: A dashboard loads a list of 200,000 sensor readings inside a setup function, and a resize handler created in that same function refers to the list. The handler stays attached for the whole time the page is open. What happens to the list?
choices: It is freed after the handler runs once, because the readings have then been used
It is freed as soon as the setup function returns, since its job is done
It stays in memory for as long as the handler exists, which can quietly increase memory use
It is copied into the handler at creation, so the original list is freed but a duplicate remains
questions.why: Anything a closure refers to stays in memory as long as the closure exists, so a long-lived handler keeps the whole large list alive.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a closure captures and give one real situation where you would use one. Include one limit or tradeoff they should watch for.
lessons.modelAnswer:
A closure is an inner function that keeps access to the variables of the scope it was created in, even after the outer function has returned. It captures the variables themselves, not copies of their values. So if one of those variables changes later, the closure sees the new value. Each call to the outer function creates fresh variables, which means two closures made by separate calls do not share state.

A real use is a counter or a cache. A makeCounter function holds a private count, and the returned function is the only way to change it. That protects the state from accidental edits.

The tradeoff is memory. Whatever a closure refers to cannot be cleaned up while the closure is still reachable. A long-lived event handler that closes over a big object keeps that object in memory. The live link can also surprise you if you expected a snapshot.
rubricPoints: Defines a closure as a function that keeps access to variables from the scope where it was defined.
States that closures capture live variables, not snapshots of their values.
Notes that each call to the outer function creates separate, independent captured state.
Gives a concrete use such as private state, a counter, a preset configuration, or a cache.
Names a limit, such as captured data staying in memory or confusion when a value is expected to be frozen.

suggested.rationale: No current mission uses JavaScript, and a JavaScript lab where the learner builds a counter factory and watches separate instances keep separate state would make closures concrete.

lessons.plain: In JavaScript, this is a hidden word inside a function that points to whichever object the function is working for at that moment. It is not fixed when you write the function. It is decided each time the function is called, by how the call is made. Think of the word "here" on a postcard: it means a different place depending on who sends it and from where. One exception is arrow functions, a shorter way to write functions. They never pick their own this. Instead, they borrow it from the surrounding code where they were written.
lessons.guessPrompt: An object `counter` has a method `show` that prints `this.count`. If you copy the method into a plain variable, `const s = counter.show;`, and then call `s()`, do you think it still prints the counter's count? Why or why not?
lessons.teach:
`this` is a value that JavaScript supplies to an ordinary function each time it runs. The call site decides it. The call site is the exact spot in the code where the function is invoked. There are five rules.

Method call: in `obj.fn()`, `this` is `obj`, the object before the dot. That object is called the receiver. Plain call: in `fn()` there is no receiver. In strict mode, an opt-in stricter setting that modules and classes use automatically, `this` is `undefined`. In older sloppy code it falls back to the global object. Explicit binding: `fn.call(x)` and `fn.apply(x)` run the function right away with `this` set to `x`. `fn.bind(x)` returns a new function whose `this` is permanently `x`. Constructor call: `new Fn()` creates a fresh object and sets `this` to that object. Arrow functions ignore all four rules. Their `this` is lexical, which means it is taken from the code surrounding the place where the arrow was written.

Worked example: `const user = { name: 'Ana', hi() { return this.name; } };`
Step 1: `user.hi()` has a receiver of `user`, so it returns 'Ana'.
Step 2: `const f = user.hi;` copies only the function. The link to `user` is not kept.
Step 3: `f()` is a plain call. In strict mode `this` is `undefined`, so reading `.name` throws a TypeError.
Step 4: `user.hi.bind(user)()` works again because `bind` fixed `this` to `user`.

A common mistake is passing a method as a callback, such as `setTimeout(user.hi, 100)` or `button.addEventListener('click', obj.handle)`. The method gets called later without its receiver. In a running app this shows up as a crash like "Cannot read properties of undefined", or as a silently wrong value. Two fixes work: wrap the call in an arrow, as in `() => user.hi()`, or use `bind`. The opposite mistake is writing an object method as an arrow function. Its `this` then comes from the surrounding code, not from the object, so it does not point to the object.

questions.prompt:
A water-plant script runs in strict mode:

const pump = { rate: 40, report() { return this.rate; } };
const backup = { rate: 15 };

Step 1: pump.report() has the receiver pump, so it returns 40.
Step 2: pump.report.call(backup) ... (missing)
Step 3: const g = pump.report.bind(backup); g() returns 15, because bind made a new function whose this is permanently backup.

Which choice correctly completes Step 2?
choices: It returns 15, because call runs report immediately with this set to backup.
It throws a TypeError, because call makes a plain call with no receiver, so this is undefined.
It returns a new function whose this is backup, and nothing runs until that function is called.
It returns 40, because report was written inside pump, so this always stays pump.
questions.why: call is explicit binding: it invokes the function right away with this set to the object you pass, so this.rate reads backup's 15.

questions.prompt: For an ordinary function (not an arrow function), what decides the value of this each time the function runs?
choices: The object the function was first written inside, fixed when the code is loaded.
The call site, meaning the exact spot where the function is invoked and how it is called.
The global object, unless the function is declared with the function keyword.
The last object that read or assigned any property inside the function body.
questions.why: For ordinary functions, this is supplied fresh on each run and is determined by how and where the function is called, not where it was defined.

choices: Object properties cannot hold functions unless they use the method shorthand show() { }.
show is an arrow function, so its this comes from the surrounding code rather than from shop.
shop.show() is a plain call, so there is no receiver and this is undefined.
The arrow needs to be invoked with new so that this becomes the shop object.
questions.why: Arrow functions ignore the method-call rule; their this is lexical, taken from the code around where the arrow was written, so it does not point to shop.

choices: tick runs with this set to the timer, so seconds is created on the timer; writing tick as an arrow fixes it.
setTimeout calls tick with new, so this is a fresh empty object; passing meter.tick.call(meter) fixes it.
tick runs without a receiver, so this is undefined and a TypeError is thrown; passing () => meter.tick() fixes it.
tick runs with this set to meter as normal, so seconds becomes 89 and no fix is needed.
questions.why: Passing meter.tick hands over only the function, so it is later called as a plain call where this is undefined in strict mode; wrapping it in an arrow keeps the receiver meter at the actual call site.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how JavaScript decides what `this` is when a function runs, and describe one concrete bug where using an arrow function versus a regular function changes the result. Name one tradeoff of arrow functions here.
lessons.modelAnswer: For a regular function, `this` isn't set when you write it. It's set by how you call it. Call it as `obj.method()` and `this` is `obj`. Call it bare, as `method()`, and in strict mode `this` is `undefined`. With `call`, `apply` or `bind` you choose it yourself, and with `new` it's the brand-new object. Arrow functions skip all of that and take `this` from the code around them. Here's a concrete bug: inside a class method I write `setTimeout(function () { this.save(); }, 100)`. The timer calls that function bare, so `this` is undefined and it crashes. If I write `setTimeout(() => this.save(), 100)` instead, the arrow keeps the class instance and it works. The tradeoff is that an arrow can't get its own `this`. So writing an object's method as an arrow is wrong, because it won't point to the object, and you can't use an arrow as a constructor either.
rubricPoints: States that a regular function's `this` is decided at call time by the call site, not where it is written.
Names the main call contexts: method call, plain call, call/apply/bind, and new.
Explains that arrow functions take `this` lexically from surrounding code.
Gives a concrete bug, such as a method passed as a callback losing its receiver.
Names a limit, such as arrows being unsuitable as object methods or constructors.

suggested.rationale: Seeing `this` change across method, plain, bound and arrow calls is best learned by running small snippets and watching the results, which the planned JavaScript lab would allow.

lessons.plain: An object in JavaScript is a labelled container: a bundle of named values kept together, like a contact card with fields for name, phone and email. An object literal is the quick way to write one directly in curly braces, listing each label (called a key) next to its value. Property access is how you read or change a value later, either with a dot followed by the label, or with square brackets holding the label as text. Shorthand syntax is a set of shortcuts that save typing when a variable already has the same name as the label you want, or when a value is a function.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose a car object has a property named color, and you also have a variable called key that holds the text "color". Do you think car.key and car[key] give the same result? Guess what each one returns and why.
lessons.teach:
An object literal is an object written out directly inside curly braces, as a list of key: value pairs separated by commas, for example { name: "Ada", age: 36 }. A key (also called a property name) is the label; it is always stored as a string. A property is one key together with its value. A method is a property whose value is a function.

There are two ways to access a property. Dot notation, user.name, uses the key written literally after the dot, so the key must be a valid identifier (letters, digits, _ or $, not starting with a digit, no spaces or hyphens). Bracket notation, user["name"], takes any expression inside the brackets, evaluates it, and uses the resulting text as the key. That makes brackets the only choice for keys like "first-name" or for keys held in a variable. Reading a key that does not exist returns undefined rather than raising an error.

Shorthand syntax trims repetition. Property shorthand: if a variable called name exists, { name } means { name: name }. Method shorthand: greet() { ... } means greet: function() { ... }. Computed property names: [expr]: value inside a literal uses the evaluated expression as the key.

Worked example. Start with const name = "Ada" and const key = "age". Build const user = { name, [key]: 36, greet() { return "Hi " + this.name; } }. Step 1: { name } becomes name: "Ada". Step 2: [key] evaluates to "age", so the property is age: 36. Step 3: greet is stored as a method. Now user.name gives "Ada", user[key] gives 36, and user.greet() returns "Hi Ada", because this inside a method called with a dot refers to the object before the dot.

The common mistake is writing user.key when you meant user[key]. Dot notation looks for a property literally named "key", finds none, and quietly returns undefined. In a running program that undefined travels onward until something tries to read a property of it and the code crashes with a "Cannot read properties of undefined" error, often far from the real cause.

questions.prompt: A weather app builds a record. It starts with const city = "Oslo" and const unit = "temp", then writes const reading = { city, [unit]: 12, summary() { return this.city + " is " + this.temp; } }. Step 1: { city } becomes city: "Oslo". Step 2: ??? Step 3: summary is stored as a method. Afterwards reading[unit] gives 12 and reading.summary() returns "Oslo is 12". Which choice correctly fills in Step 2?
choices: The key is written literally, so the property is unit: 12
[unit] is evaluated to "temp", so the property is temp: 12
The key keeps its brackets, so the property is "[unit]": 12
The value is used as the key, so the property is 12: "temp"
questions.why: A computed property name evaluates the expression in the square brackets and uses the result, here "temp", as the key.

questions.prompt: A shipping company stores parcels as objects with a key named "order-id", for example const parcel = { "order-id": 5521 }. Which expression reads that value correctly?
choices: parcel.order-id
parcel."order-id"
parcel.orderid
parcel["order-id"]
questions.why: "order-id" contains a hyphen, so it is not a valid identifier and must be read with bracket notation.

questions.prompt: A library tracks copies with const field = "copies" and const shelf = { copies: 8 }. A developer writes const count = shelf.field. What is stored in count?
choices: An error is raised immediately
undefined
"copies"
questions.why: Dot notation looks for a property literally named "field", which does not exist, so it quietly returns undefined; shelf[field] would give 8.

questions.prompt: A bookshop has const title = "Dune" and const pages = 412. Which object literal is exactly the same as const book = { title, pages }?
choices: { title: title, pages: pages }
{ "title": "title", "pages": "pages" }
{ [title]: title, [pages]: pages }
questions.why: Property shorthand { title } means title: title, so each key is the variable's name and each value is the variable's value.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would build an object with a literal and read its properties, when they should use dot versus bracket notation, and what shorthand saves them. Name at least one limit or trap they should watch out for.
lessons.modelAnswer: An object literal is a set of key: value pairs in curly braces, like { name: "Ada", age: 36 }; keys are stored as strings. To read a value, use dot notation (user.name) when the key is a fixed, valid identifier, because it is short and readable. Use bracket notation (user["first-name"] or user[key]) when the key has spaces or hyphens, or when it lives in a variable, because brackets evaluate what is inside them. Shorthand helps: { name } copies a same-named variable, greet() { } defines a method, and [key]: value computes a key. The tradeoff is that dot notation is cleaner but cannot handle dynamic or unusual keys. The main trap is writing user.key when you meant user[key]: it looks up a property literally called "key", returns undefined without any error, and the program fails later somewhere confusing.
rubricPoints: An object literal is key: value pairs inside curly braces, with keys stored as strings.
Dot notation needs a literal, valid identifier key; bracket notation evaluates an expression and handles any key.
Property shorthand { name } means name: name, and method shorthand defines a function property.
Computed keys [expr]: value use the evaluated expression as the property name.
Missing properties return undefined silently, so confusing obj.key with obj[key] causes bugs that surface later.

suggested.rationale: Building objects and comparing dot, bracket and shorthand results is best learned by running small snippets in a JavaScript lab and watching undefined appear when access goes wrong.

lessons.plain: Every JavaScript array (an ordered list of values) comes with built-in tools that walk through the list for you, so you don't write the loop by hand. Each tool takes a small function you supply and applies it to each item. map transforms every item into something new. filter keeps only the items that pass a test. reduce boils the whole list down to one value, like a total. find returns the first matching item. some asks whether any item passes, and every asks whether all of them do. Think of an assembly line: each station does one simple job, and you chain stations together.
lessons.guessPrompt: You have a list of 1,000 orders and want to know whether at least one is unpaid. The very first order you check is unpaid. Do you need to keep checking the other 999? Why or why not?
lessons.teach:
An array method is a function built into every array. The methods here each take a callback, which is a function you pass in that the method calls once per element (one item in the array). None of them changes the original array.

map returns a new array of the same length, where each slot holds whatever your callback returned for that element. filter returns a new array containing only the elements for which your callback returned a truthy value (anything JavaScript treats as true). reduce carries an accumulator, a running result, through the array. Your callback receives the accumulator and the current element and returns the next accumulator. The second argument to reduce is the initial value. find returns the first element that passes your test, or undefined if none does. some returns true as soon as one element passes. every returns false as soon as one fails. Both stop early, which is called short-circuiting. Note that every returns true on an empty array, because nothing failed.

Worked example. Take orders: {total: 20, paid: true}, {total: 50, paid: false}, {total: 30, paid: true}. To sum the paid totals, chain orders.filter(o => o.paid).map(o => o.total).reduce((sum, t) => sum + t, 0). Step 1: filter keeps the first and third orders. Step 2: map turns them into [20, 30]. Step 3: reduce starts sum at 0. It adds 20 to get 20, then adds 30 to get 50. The result is 50. Separately, orders.some(o => !o.paid) returns true when it reaches the second order and never looks at the third.

Common mistake: writing an arrow function with curly braces but no return, as in o => { o.total }. The callback then returns undefined. map produces [undefined, undefined], and filter keeps nothing. In a running app this shows up as blank fields or empty lists, with no error message to warn you. A related trap is calling reduce on an empty array without an initial value, which throws a TypeError.

questions.prompt: A tutoring centre stores test scores as [72, 45, 88, 91]. It wants to give each passing score (60 or above) a 5-point bonus and then add up the results. The code is scores.filter(s => s >= 60).map(s => s + 5).reduce((acc, s) => acc + s, 0). Step 1: filter keeps only the elements where the callback returns a truthy value, so it keeps 72, 88 and 91.
