Step 2: (missing). Step 3: reduce starts the accumulator at 0. It adds 77 to get 77, then 93 to get 170, then 96 to get 266. The result is 266. Which statement correctly fills in Step 2?
choices: map turns them into [true, true, true] because every callback result is truthy
map turns the scores into [77, 50, 93, 96] by adding 5 to every score in the original list
map turns the filtered scores into a new array, [77, 93, 96], the same length as the array it was called on
map changes the scores array itself, so scores now holds [77, 93, 96]
questions.why: map works on the array that filter returned, which has three elements, and it returns a new array of the same length that holds each callback result (score + 5), without changing the original scores array.

questions.prompt: A help desk has tickets = [{id: 1, priority: 'low'}, {id: 2, priority: 'high'}, {id: 3, priority: 'high'}]. What does tickets.find(t => t.priority === 'high') return?
choices: [{id: 2, priority: 'high'}, {id: 3, priority: 'high'}]
{id: 3, priority: 'high'}
{id: 2, priority: 'high'}
true
questions.why: find returns only the first element that passes the test, which is ticket 2. It does not return an array of all matches, as filter would, and it does not return a true/false answer, as some would.

questions.prompt: A warehouse monitoring app has not registered any sensors yet, so sensors = []. What does sensors.every(s => s.online) return?
choices: false
undefined
It throws a TypeError
true
questions.why: every returns false only when an element fails the test. An empty array has no elements, so nothing can fail, and every returns true.

questions.prompt: A developer writes ['ana', 'raj'].map(n => { n.toUpperCase() }) to make a list of capitalised user names for a page. What does this produce?
choices: ['ANA', 'RAJ']
A TypeError, because the callback is missing a return
An empty array []
[undefined, undefined]
questions.why: Because the arrow function has curly braces but no return statement, the callback returns undefined for each element. map still builds a new array of the same length, so it produces [undefined, undefined] without any error message.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how map, filter, reduce, find, some and every differ, using what each one returns. Name one limit or tradeoff of chaining them instead of writing a single loop.
lessons.modelAnswer: All six take a callback and leave the original array alone. The difference is what comes back. map gives a new array of the same length, with each element transformed. filter gives a new array holding only the elements that passed the test. reduce folds everything into one value using an accumulator, and you should always give it a starting value so an empty array doesn't throw. find gives the first match or undefined. some and every give a boolean, and both stop early once the answer is known. One gotcha is that every returns true on an empty array. Chaining reads clearly, because each step does one job. The tradeoff is that each step makes another pass over the data and builds an intermediate array. On very large data, or in hot code paths, that can cost more than one loop. Also, a long reduce can become harder to read than the loop it replaced.
rubricPoints: States what each method returns: new array (map, filter), single value (reduce), element or undefined (find), boolean (some, every).
Explains that the callback runs per element and the original array is not modified.
Describes the reduce accumulator and the importance of an initial value.
Notes that some and every short-circuit, or that every is true on an empty array.
Names a tradeoff such as extra passes and intermediate arrays, or reduce hurting readability.

suggested.rationale: These methods are learned best by running chains on real nested data and seeing each intermediate result, which a JavaScript lab would provide.

lessons.plain: Destructuring is a shortcut for pulling several values out of an object or a list and giving each one its own named variable, all in one line. Think of unpacking a delivery box that has labelled compartments: instead of reaching in one item at a time and naming each, you hold up a cut-out that matches the box's layout, and every item drops into its matching slot. With objects, values are matched by their label (the property name). With lists, called arrays, values are matched by their place in line (first, second, and so on). The result is shorter, clearer code that shows exactly which pieces of the data you care about.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose an object holds { city: 'Lima', zip: '15001' } and you write const { zip, city } = thatObject, listing zip before city. Which value do you think ends up in the variable city, and why?
lessons.teach:
Destructuring assignment is syntax that unpacks values from an object or array into separate variables in one statement. The pattern on the left of the equals sign mirrors the shape of the data on the right. Object destructuring uses curly braces and matches by property name, where a property is a named value stored on an object. So const { name, age } = user creates variables name and age from user.name and user.age, and order does not matter. Array destructuring uses square brackets and matches by position, called the index, which counts from 0. So const [first, second] = list takes index 0 and index 1. You can skip an array slot by leaving it empty, as in const [, second] = list. You can rename while unpacking, as in const { name: userName } = user. You can give a default, a fallback used only when the value is undefined, as in const { role = 'guest' } = user. You can also nest patterns to reach inside nested data.

Why it works: JavaScript reads the pattern as instructions. For each name in braces it looks up that property, and for each slot in brackets it looks up that index. It then assigns the results. It is shorthand for several property-access lines written by hand.

Worked example. Data: const order = { id: 7, customer: { name: 'Ana' }, items: ['pen', 'ink'] }. Statement: const { id, customer: { name }, items: [firstItem] } = order. Step 1: id matches order.id, so id is 7. Step 2: customer: { name } looks up order.customer and then destructures that inner object, so name is 'Ana'. No variable called customer is created. Step 3: items: [firstItem] looks up order.items and takes index 0, so firstItem is 'pen'.

Common mistake: destructuring a nested part that is missing. If order had no customer property, the pattern tries to read name from undefined and throws a TypeError. In a running program, one record with a missing field can crash a whole loop or request handler. Guard against this with a default for the nested object, such as customer: { name } = {}. A missing customer then leaves name as undefined instead of throwing an error.

questions.prompt: A library app stores this record: const book = { title: 'Dune', author: { last: 'Herbert' }, tags: ['scifi', 'classic', 'novel'] }. It runs: const { title, author: { last: authorLast }, tags: [, secondTag] } = book. Step 1: title matches book.title, so title is 'Dune'. Step 2: (missing). Step 3: tags: [, secondTag] looks up book.tags, skips index 0 because that slot is left empty, and takes index 1, so secondTag is 'classic'. Which choice correctly fills in Step 2?
choices: author: { last: authorLast } looks up book.author, then reads its last property and stores it under the new name authorLast, so authorLast is 'Herbert'. No author or last variable is created.
author: { last: authorLast } looks for a property called authorLast inside book.author, finds none, and leaves authorLast as undefined.
author: { last: authorLast } creates a variable called author that holds { last: 'Herbert' }, and authorLast is also 'Herbert'.
author: { last: authorLast } looks up book.author, then reads its last property, so a variable called last is created holding 'Herbert'.
questions.why: In a nested pattern, author: only says where to look, and last: authorLast reads the property last and renames it, so only authorLast is created and it holds 'Herbert'.

questions.prompt: A shop runs: const { qty, price } = { price: 4, qty: 9 }. What is the value of qty afterwards?
choices: A TypeError is thrown because the order does not match
undefined, because qty is listed first but price comes first in the object
questions.why: Object destructuring matches by property name, not by order, so qty takes the value of the qty property, which is 9.

questions.prompt: A sensor log runs: const [, , third = 0] = [5, 8]. What is the value of third?
choices: undefined
questions.why: The two empty slots skip index 0 and index 1. Index 2 does not exist, so it is undefined, and the default of 0 is used.

questions.prompt: A delivery service has the record const shipment = { id: 'S-12' }, with no carrier property. It runs: const { carrier: { phone } } = shipment. What happens, and what would prevent it?
choices: A variable called carrier is created as an empty object, and phone is undefined.
phone is set to null. Adding a default with phone = '' would prevent this.
A TypeError is thrown because the pattern tries to read phone from undefined. Writing carrier: { phone } = {} would leave phone as undefined instead.
phone is set to undefined, and nothing needs to change.
questions.why: shipment.carrier is undefined, so reading phone from it throws a TypeError. A default of {} for the nested object gives the pattern something safe to read from.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate keeps writing three separate lines like const id = order.id to pull values out of objects and arrays. Explain to them in your own words what destructuring does, how object and array destructuring differ, and name one limit or risk they should watch for.
lessons.modelAnswer: Destructuring lets you unpack several values from an object or array into named variables in one statement. You write a pattern that mirrors the data's shape. For an object, use curly braces. Values are matched by property name, so const { id, total } = order works no matter what order you list them in. For an array, use square brackets. Values are matched by position, so const [first, second] = list takes index 0 and index 1. You can rename a value, give it a default for when it is undefined, skip array slots, and nest patterns to reach deeper data. The risk is nested data that is missing. If you destructure customer: { name } and customer is undefined, JavaScript throws a TypeError, and that can crash a loop over many records. Add a default like customer: { name } = {} when a field might be absent. Also keep patterns readable, because deep nesting gets hard to follow.
rubricPoints: Destructuring unpacks values from objects or arrays into separate variables in one statement, using a pattern that mirrors the data's shape.
Object destructuring matches by property name, so the order of the names does not matter.
Array destructuring matches by position (index), and slots can be skipped.
Defaults apply only when a value is undefined, and properties can be renamed while unpacking.
Destructuring a missing nested object throws a TypeError, so risky nested patterns need a default such as = {}.

suggested.rationale: Destructuring is learned fastest by running patterns against real nested data and watching what each variable receives or which TypeError appears, and the planned JavaScript lab would let learners do exactly that.

lessons.plain: Spread and rest are two uses of the same three dots (...) in JavaScript. Spread unpacks a group into its separate pieces, the way you tip a bag of groceries out onto a table. You use it to copy or merge arrays (ordered lists) and objects (collections of named values). Rest does the opposite. It gathers leftover pieces back into one bag, so a function can accept any number of arguments, or you can collect 'everything else' from a list. The dots look identical. Where they sit tells you which job they are doing.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose you have two settings objects. The first says the color is red and the second says the color is blue. You combine them by unpacking the first and then the second into one new object. Which color do you think the combined object ends up with, and why?
lessons.teach:
Spread syntax (...) expands an array or object into its individual items. An array is an ordered list of values. An object is a set of key-value pairs called properties. Spread is used where values are being written out, such as inside [ ] or { } literals or in a function call. Rest syntax uses the same dots to collect several items into one new array or object. It appears where values are being received, such as in a function's parameter list or on the left side of a destructuring assignment. Destructuring means pulling values out into variables.

This works because the engine copies items one at a time in reading order. When two object properties share a key, the later one overwrites the earlier one.

Here is a worked example. Start with const base = { host: 'db', port: 80 } and const cfg = { ...base, port: 8080 }. Step 1: the spread copies host: 'db' into the new object. Step 2: it copies port: 80. Step 3: the literal port: 8080 comes next and overwrites port, giving { host: 'db', port: 8080 }.

Arrays work the same way: [...[1, 2], 3] gives [1, 2, 3]. For rest, take function total(...nums). Calling total(4, 5, 6) collects the arguments into the array nums = [4, 5, 6]. A rest element must come last, because it takes everything that remains.

A common mistake is putting the override first, as in { port: 8080, ...base }. The spread runs after the override, so port becomes 80 again. In a running system, a configuration override is then silently ignored. The service may connect to the wrong port, and no error is raised.

Spread also copies only one level deep. A nested object inside the copy is still the same object as in the original. Changing it through the copy changes the original too.

questions.prompt: A library app merges reader preferences. Start with const defaults = { theme: 'light', lang: 'en', size: 12 } and const reader = { lang: 'fr' }. Then const prefs = { ...defaults, ...reader }. Step 1: spreading defaults copies theme: 'light'. Step 2: it copies lang: 'en'. Step 3: it copies size: 12. Step 4: ??? Result: { theme: 'light', lang: 'fr', size: 12 }. Which choice correctly describes Step 4?
choices: Spreading reader adds a second lang key, so the object holds both 'en' and 'fr'
Spreading reader copies lang: 'fr', which overwrites the earlier lang: 'en'
Spreading reader throws an error because two properties share the key lang
Spreading reader is skipped because lang already exists in the new object
questions.why: Items are copied in reading order, and when two properties share a key the later one overwrites the earlier one, so lang becomes 'fr'.

questions.prompt: A scoreboard stores lap times as const laps = [7, 8, 9]. A developer writes const [first, ...others] = laps. What is others, and what is the ... doing here?
choices: others is 8, and the ... is spread expanding the array
others is [7, 8, 9], and the ... is spread copying the whole array
others is [8, 9], and the ... is rest collecting the remaining items
others is [9], and the ... is rest taking only the last item
questions.why: On the left side of a destructuring assignment the dots are rest syntax, which collects everything left after first into a new array, [8, 9].

questions.prompt: A shipping service has const standard = { qty: 1, speed: 'slow' }. To make a rush order a developer writes const rush = { speed: 'fast', ...standard }. What is rush.speed, and why?
choices: An error is raised because speed appears twice in the literal
'fast', because properties written by hand always win over spread ones
'slow', because the spread runs after the override and overwrites it
'fast', because spread skips keys that are already present
questions.why: Items are copied in reading order, so standard is spread after speed: 'fast' and its speed: 'slow' overwrites the override with no error raised.

questions.prompt: A sports club has const team = { name: 'Hawks', coach: { name: 'Kim' } }. A developer makes const copy = { ...team } and then runs copy.coach.name = 'Lee'. What is team.coach.name now?
choices: 'Kim', because changing a copy can never affect the original
undefined, because the nested coach object was not copied at all
'Lee', because spread copies only one level deep and coach is shared
'Kim', because spread made a fully independent copy of team
questions.why: Spread copies only one level deep, so copy.coach is the same object as team.coach and changing it through the copy changes the original.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between spread and rest, using a config-merge example. Include one limit or trap they should watch for.
lessons.modelAnswer: Both use three dots, and position decides the meaning. Spread sits where values are produced, inside an array or object literal or a function call, and unpacks items. Rest sits where values are received, in parameters or destructuring, and gathers leftovers into a new array or object. Rest must be last. To merge configs, I write { ...defaults, ...overrides }. Items are copied left to right, and later keys overwrite earlier ones, so the overrides win. If you flip the order, your overrides get silently replaced by defaults and nothing errors. The other trap is that spread is shallow. A nested object, like a database settings object inside the config, is shared between the copy and the original. Editing it through the copy changes the original too.
rubricPoints: Spread expands an array or object into individual items, and rest collects items into one array or object.
The same three dots are used, and position (producing vs receiving values) decides the meaning.
In object spread, later properties overwrite earlier ones, so order matters for merges.
A rest element must be the last one in the parameter list or pattern.
Spread makes only a shallow copy, so nested objects stay shared.

suggested.rationale: Predicting and then checking merge order, rest parameters and shallow-copy effects in a live JavaScript lab builds this skill best.

lessons.plain: In JavaScript, a variable holding an object or array does not hold the thing itself; it holds a pointer to where the thing lives, like a house address written on a card. Copying the card gives you a second card with the same address, not a second house. A shallow copy builds a new house but keeps the same furniture, so nested items are still shared. A deep copy rebuilds the house and every piece of furniture inside it. Knowing which copy you have tells you whether changing your version will quietly change someone else's.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you write let a = { score: 1 }; let b = a; and then set b.score = 5, what do you think a.score is now, and why?
lessons.teach:
A primitive is a simple value such as a number, string or boolean; assigning it copies the value itself. An object (including arrays) is stored by reference: the variable holds a reference, meaning a pointer to one shared object in memory. Assigning or passing that variable copies only the pointer, so two names can point at the same object.

A shallow copy creates a new outer object and copies each top-level property. Primitive properties become independent, but any property that is itself an object is copied as a reference, so nested objects stay shared. Spread syntax ({ ...obj } or [...arr], which unpacks an object's or array's entries into a new one) and Object.assign both make shallow copies. A deep copy recursively copies every level, so nothing is shared. The built-in structuredClone(obj) does this; JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj)) also works for plain data but drops functions and undefined, and turns dates into strings.

Worked example. Start with const user = { name: 'Ana', tags: ['admin'] }. Step 1: const copy = { ...user } creates a new outer object, so copy !== user. Step 2: copy.name = 'Ben' changes only copy, because name was a primitive copied by value; user.name is still 'Ana'. Step 3: copy.tags.push('dev') follows the shared reference to the one tags array, so user.tags is now ['admin', 'dev'] too. Step 4: with const deep = structuredClone(user), deep.tags.push('ops') leaves user.tags untouched.

Common mistake: assuming spread means fully independent, then editing a nested array inside the copy. Also, const only stops reassigning the variable; it does not freeze the object it points to.

In a running system this causes action-at-a-distance bugs: a function that tweaks its argument silently corrupts the caller's data, a shared default config is altered for every later user, or a UI fails to refresh because the outer object never changed identity. Copying the levels you change, and returning new objects instead of mutating inputs, prevents these bugs.

questions.prompt: A bakery app stores a shopping cart as an array of objects: const cart = [{ item: 'bagel', qty: 1 }, { item: 'muffin', qty: 3 }]. A developer writes const draft = [...cart]. Step 1: draft is a new outer array, so draft !== cart. Step 2: draft.push({ item: 'scone', qty: 5 }) adds to draft only, so cart.length is still 2. Step 3: draft[0].qty = 6 runs. What is true about cart after Step 3? (Step 4 would be to use structuredClone(cart) instead, so that changing a nested item no longer affects cart.)
choices: cart[0].qty is still 1, because the spread copy gave draft its own independent item objects.
Step 3 throws an error, because cart was declared with const and cannot be changed.
cart[0].qty is now 6, because draft[0] and cart[0] point to the same shared item object.
cart.length becomes 3, because draft and cart are the same array after spreading.
questions.why: Spread makes a shallow copy, so the outer array is new but each item object inside it is copied only as a reference and is still shared with cart.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes a shallow copy of an object in JavaScript?
choices: A new outer object whose top-level properties are copied, while any nested objects are still shared by reference.
A copy that only keeps primitive properties and leaves out any nested objects or arrays.
A second variable that holds the same reference as the original, so both names point at one object.
A copy that duplicates every level of nesting, so the copy shares nothing with the original.
questions.why: A shallow copy creates a new outer object, but properties that are themselves objects are copied as references, so nested objects remain shared.

questions.prompt: A ticketing service has const defaults = { retries: 2, headers: { lang: 'en' } }. A helper does this: function makeConfig(lang) { const c = Object.assign({}, defaults); c.headers.lang = lang; return c; }. The code calls makeConfig('fr'). What is defaults.headers.lang afterwards?
choices: 'fr', because Object.assign copies only the top level, so c.headers is the same object as defaults.headers.
'en', because defaults was declared with const, which prevents its properties from changing.
undefined, because Object.assign moves the headers property out of defaults into c.
'en', because Object.assign creates a new object, so all changes to c are independent of defaults.
questions.why: Object.assign makes a shallow copy, so the nested headers object is shared and editing it through c also changes the shared default config.

questions.prompt: A calendar app copies an event with JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(event)), where event = { title: 'Launch', when: new Date(2025, 0, 15), remind: function () {}, note: undefined }. What does the resulting copy look like?
choices: A shallow copy in which when is still shared by reference with the original event.
The copy has title and when, but when is now a string, and remind and note are missing.
An exact deep copy, with when still a Date, remind still a function and note still undefined.
The copy has title only, because JSON drops every property that is not a string.
questions.why: The JSON round trip deep-copies plain data, but it drops functions and undefined values and turns dates into strings.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why changing a copied object sometimes changes the original too, and when you would choose a shallow copy over a deep copy, naming one limit or cost of each.
lessons.modelAnswer: Objects and arrays live in memory once, and variables just hold a reference to them, so b = a gives two names for the same object; changing b changes a. A shallow copy, like spread or Object.assign, makes a new outer object, so top-level primitive fields are independent, but nested objects and arrays are still shared, so editing copy.tags edits the original's tags. A deep copy, such as structuredClone, duplicates every level so nothing is shared. I use a shallow copy when I only change top-level fields or I replace nested parts with new objects; it is cheap but leaves nesting shared. I use a deep copy when I must change nested data freely; it costs more time and memory on big structures, and the JSON trick loses functions, undefined and real dates.
rubricPoints: Objects and arrays are held by reference, so assignment copies the pointer, not the data.
Primitives are copied by value and are independent after assignment.
A shallow copy (spread, Object.assign) creates a new top level but shares nested objects.
A deep copy (structuredClone) duplicates every level so nothing is shared.
Names a tradeoff: shallow is cheap but leaves shared nesting; deep costs more and JSON-based copying loses some types.
Connects to a real bug, such as a function mutating its caller's data.

suggested.rationale: Seeing a nested mutation leak back into the original in a live JavaScript lab makes reference semantics stick far better than reading about it.

lessons.plain: A web page, once loaded, is held by the browser as a family tree of boxes called the DOM (Document Object Model): the page contains a body, the body contains sections, sections contain buttons and paragraphs. Selecting means finding the exact box you want so your code can read or change it. Traversing means moving around the tree from a box you already have: up to its parent, down to its children, or sideways to its siblings. It is like finding a person in a family tree, then asking 'who is your mother?' or 'who are your children?' instead of searching the whole tree again.
lessons.guessPrompt: You have a 'Delete' button sitting inside a card on a page full of cards. Without searching the whole page, how would you find the specific card that this button belongs to?
lessons.teach:
The DOM is the browser's tree of objects for the page. Each tag becomes an element node, and every element has one parent and zero or more children. JavaScript reaches this tree through the global document object.

To select, document.querySelector(selector) returns the first element matching a CSS selector (such as '#cart', '.item' or 'ul > li'), or null if nothing matches. document.querySelectorAll(selector) returns a NodeList, a list-like collection of every match. Both also work on any element, which limits the search to that element's descendants (the elements nested anywhere inside it).

To traverse from an element you already hold, use these. element.parentElement gives its direct parent. element.children gives its child elements in order. firstElementChild and lastElementChild give the first and last child element. nextElementSibling and previousElementSibling give the neighbour elements that share the same parent. element.closest(selector) climbs upward, starting with the element itself, and returns the nearest ancestor that matches, or null.

This works because the tree's structure mirrors the layout, so relationships stay stable even when there are many repeated cards.

Worked example. Take this markup: div.card containing h3 'Mug' and button.delete. Step 1: const btn = document.querySelector('.delete') gives the first delete button. Step 2: btn.closest('.card') checks the button itself (no match), then its parent div.card (match), and returns it. Step 3: card.querySelector('h3').textContent reads 'Mug'. The search is scoped to this one card, so you get this card's title and not another card's.

A common mistake is assuming querySelector returns all matches, or forgetting it can return null. Calling a method on null throws a TypeError, which stops the rest of your script, so a page feature silently breaks. A related trap is using childNodes or nextSibling, which include text nodes made from whitespace, instead of the 'Element' versions, which skip them.

questions.prompt: A library site lists loans. Each loan is an li with class 'loan'. Inside each li are span.title, span.due and a div.actions that holds button.renew. You already hold the renew button of the second loan in a variable named renewBtn. Its loan is 'Dune', due '12 May'. The goal is to read that loan's due date and no other. Step 1: renewBtn holds the second loan's button (given). Step 2: const loan = ______ ; Step 3: loan.querySelector('.due').textContent reads '12 May', because the search is scoped to this one li. Which expression completes Step 2?
choices: document.querySelector('.loan')
renewBtn.closest('.due')
renewBtn.parentElement
renewBtn.closest('.loan')
questions.why: closest('.loan') climbs up from the button, through div.actions, to the nearest li.loan that contains it, so the scoped search in Step 3 finds this loan's due date.

questions.prompt: A shop page runs this line first: document.querySelector('#checkout-btn').addEventListener('click', pay). The button's id in the markup is actually 'checkoutButton'. More setup code follows that line. What happens?
choices: querySelector falls back to the closest-named element, so the click handler still attaches
Only that line is skipped, and the code after it still runs normally
querySelector returns null, calling addEventListener on null throws a TypeError, and the rest of the script stops
querySelector returns an empty NodeList, and addEventListener quietly does nothing
questions.why: querySelector returns null when nothing matches, and calling a method on null throws a TypeError that halts the remaining code.

questions.prompt: A recipe page has an ol whose li elements are written on separate lines in the HTML: 'Preheat oven', then 'Mix flour'. You hold the 'Preheat oven' li in a variable named step. Which expression reliably gives you the 'Mix flour' li?
choices: step.nextSibling
step.parentElement.firstElementChild
step.childNodes[1]
step.nextElementSibling
questions.why: nextElementSibling skips whitespace text nodes and returns the next element with the same parent. nextSibling may return the whitespace text node instead.

questions.prompt: A dashboard has a section with class 'panel'. Nested inside it is a div with classes 'panel active'. You hold that div in a variable named box. What does box.closest('.panel') return?
choices: null, because the div matches but is not an ancestor of itself
The div itself, because closest starts by checking the element it is called on
The outer section, because closest only looks at ancestors
A NodeList containing both the div and the section
questions.why: closest checks the starting element first. The div already matches '.panel', so it returns the div before climbing any higher.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between selecting with querySelector and traversing with closest or parent/child properties, and name one limit or risk of each approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: querySelector searches downward from the document, or from an element, using a CSS selector and gives back the first match. querySelectorAll gives every match as a NodeList. That is how you find a starting point. Traversal moves from an element you already hold. parentElement and closest go up, children goes down, and the nextElementSibling and previousElementSibling properties go sideways. closest is the one I use when a button needs its own card, because it climbs to the nearest matching ancestor. The limit of querySelector is that it only returns the first match. It also returns null when nothing matches, and calling a method on null throws an error and stops the script. Traversal has its own risk: it depends on the markup's structure. If someone wraps the button in an extra div, parentElement now points at the wrong node. closest with a clear selector survives that kind of change much better.
rubricPoints: querySelector returns the first CSS-selector match or null, and querySelectorAll returns all matches.
Selection can be scoped by calling querySelector on an element instead of on document.
closest climbs upward from the element itself to the nearest matching ancestor.
parentElement, children and the sibling properties move one step through the tree.
Unhandled null results cause errors, and relying on exact parent positions is fragile when markup changes.

suggested.rationale: Selecting and traversing a real DOM tree is a hands-on skill best built by running code in a JavaScript lab, and no current mission covers browser JavaScript.

lessons.plain: A web page, once loaded, lives in the browser as a tree of objects called the DOM (Document Object Model). Each piece, like a heading, a paragraph or a list item, is a node in that tree. JavaScript can grow this tree by making new nodes and attaching them, change existing nodes by editing their text, classes or attributes, and prune it by removing nodes. Think of a family tree on a whiteboard. You can write a new name and draw a line to its parent, cross out and rewrite a name, or erase a branch. The screen redraws to match the tree.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose you write code that builds a brand-new list item with the text 'Buy milk' but never attaches it to the shopping list already on the page. Would the user see 'Buy milk'? Why or why not?
lessons.teach:
The DOM is the browser's live tree of objects that represents the page. A node is any item in that tree. An element is a node for a tag such as li or p. Changing the tree changes what the user sees, because the browser re-renders, or redraws, from the tree. To create a node, call document.createElement('li'). This returns an element that exists only in memory. It is not on the page until you attach it to a parent already in the tree, using parent.append(child). To modify a node, set el.textContent, which replaces the node's text and treats it as plain text. You can also use el.classList.add('done') to add a CSS class (a style hook), or el.setAttribute('data-id', '7') to set an attribute, which is a named value on the tag. To remove a node, call el.remove(), which detaches it and everything inside it. Worked example: a page has an empty list, ul#todos. First, list = document.querySelector('#todos') finds the list. Second, item = document.createElement('li') makes a detached li. Third, item.textContent = 'Buy milk' gives it text, though it is still invisible. Fourth, list.append(item) attaches it, and now 'Buy milk' appears. Fifth, item.classList.add('done') may restyle it, for example with a strike-through. Sixth, item.remove() makes it disappear, while the variable item still holds the detached object in memory. A common mistake is building content with innerHTML from user input, for example list.innerHTML += '
  • ' + userText + '
    • '. innerHTML parses the string as HTML. A user could then inject markup or scripts, which is a security hole called cross-site scripting. Using += with innerHTML also rebuilds every existing child, so any listeners you attached to the old children are lost. Prefer createElement plus textContent for anything containing user data. In a running app, this keeps the page safe and keeps existing nodes and their behaviour intact.

questions.prompt: A bakery's order page has an empty container, div#cart, already in the page. A customer clicks to add an item, and this code runs. Step 1: cart = document.querySelector('#cart') finds the container. Step 2: row = document.createElement('p') makes a new paragraph element that exists only in memory. Step 3: row.textContent = '3 croissants' gives it plain text, but nothing shows on the page yet. Step 4: [missing]. Afterwards, '3 croissants' is visible. Step 5: row.setAttribute('data-sku', '42') stores a product code on the tag. Which line belongs at Step 4?
choices: cart.append(row)
No line is needed, because setting textContent in Step 3 already shows it
row.append(cart)
cart.innerHTML += row
questions.why: A created element stays detached until you attach it to a parent that is already in the tree, and parent.append(child) does that with cart as the parent and row as the child.

questions.prompt:
A community guestbook shows visitor names inside div#board. A developer adds each new name with board.innerHTML += '

' + visitorName + '

', where visitorName is whatever the visitor typed. Earlier entries had click listeners attached. Which statement best describes the problems with this approach?
choices: It is safe because innerHTML treats everything as plain text, but it is slower than append
The only problem is that the new paragraph stays detached in memory until append is called
It works correctly, but the new paragraph cannot be given a CSS class later
The typed text is parsed as HTML, so a visitor could inject markup or scripts (cross-site scripting), and += rebuilds all existing children, which loses their listeners
questions.why: innerHTML parses its string as HTML, which allows injection, and using += rebuilds every existing child, so listeners attached to the old children are lost.

questions.prompt: On a library website, a variable banner holds a div that is on the page and contains two paragraphs. The code runs banner.remove(). What is true afterwards?
choices: The div is hidden but still in the tree, so it can be shown again with a CSS class
The div and both paragraphs leave the page, and the banner variable still holds the detached object
Only the div is removed, and its two paragraphs stay visible on the page
The div and the banner variable are both erased from memory immediately
questions.why: remove() detaches the node and everything inside it from the tree, but the variable still refers to the detached object in memory.

questions.prompt: A gym's class schedule page runs slot.textContent = 'Yoga 6pm' on an element that is already on the page. What does the user see in that element?
choices: Only 6pm, because the tags and the text between them are removed
The word Yoga in bold, followed by 6pm
The literal characters Yoga 6pm, angle brackets included
Nothing, because textContent only works on detached elements
questions.why: textContent replaces the node's text and treats it as plain text, so the tags are shown as characters instead of being parsed as HTML.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks why you used createElement, textContent and append to add rows to a table instead of one innerHTML string. Explain in your own words how creating, modifying and removing nodes works, and name the tradeoff between the two approaches.
lessons.modelAnswer: The page is a live tree of nodes, and whatever the tree holds is what the browser draws. createElement makes a new element in memory, but nothing shows until I append it to a parent that is already on the page. I set its text with textContent, which treats the value strictly as text, so a user typing angle brackets can't inject HTML or script. I change looks with classList or setAttribute, and I call remove() to take a node out. innerHTML is shorter and handy for big static chunks of markup, but it parses strings as HTML. That opens a cross-site scripting risk with user data. Using += also rebuilds all the existing children, so their event listeners are lost. The tradeoff is more lines of code in exchange for safety and stable existing nodes.
rubricPoints: The DOM is a live tree, and changing it changes what is displayed.
createElement makes a detached node that only appears after being appended to a parent on the page.
textContent, classList and setAttribute modify an existing node.
remove() detaches a node and its children.
innerHTML with user input risks script injection and rebuilds existing children, losing their listeners.
Names a tradeoff, such as innerHTML being more concise versus createElement being safer.

suggested.rationale: Building, editing and removing nodes is a hands-on skill best learned by running code in a JavaScript lab and watching the page tree change.

lessons.plain: When someone clicks, types or submits something on a web page, the browser creates an event, a small report of what just happened. An event listener is a function you attach to an element so it runs when that kind of event reaches it. Events do not touch only one element. They travel down from the top of the page to the clicked element, which is called capturing, then back up through its containers, which is called bubbling. Picture a letter going building, floor, apartment, then an echo coming back up. Because of bubbling, one listener on a parent can handle many children, which is called delegation. Some events also trigger a built-in browser action that you can cancel.
lessons.guessPrompt: A list holds 50 buttons, and you attach one click listener to the list itself, not to any button. When a user clicks the 20th button, do you expect the list's listener to run? Why or why not?
lessons.teach:
An event is an object the browser creates when something happens, such as a click or a form submit. An event listener is a function you register with element.addEventListener(type, handler), and the browser calls it with that event object. Two properties matter most. event.target is the element where the event actually started, the innermost thing clicked. event.currentTarget is the element whose listener is running right now.

Events travel in three phases. In the capturing phase the event moves from the document down through each ancestor (any containing element) toward the target. In the target phase it arrives at the target. In the bubbling phase it travels back up through each ancestor. By default, listeners run during bubbling. Passing { capture: true } as the third argument makes a listener run on the way down instead. Calling event.stopPropagation() halts the journey, so later ancestors never receive the event.

Delegation relies on bubbling. You put one listener on a shared parent and inspect event.target to decide what was clicked, instead of adding a listener to every child. This also covers children added later.

Worked example: a list with id todos holds items, and each item has a delete button. One click listener sits on the list. It calls event.target.closest('button.delete'), where closest walks up from an element to the nearest match. If that returns nothing, the listener stops. Otherwise it removes the button's item. Trace a click on the third delete button. Capturing passes document, body, list and item. The target is the button. Bubbling goes button, item, list, and the list's listener fires. closest finds the button, and its item is removed. A click on an item's text gives no match, so nothing happens.

preventDefault() cancels the browser's built-in action for an event, such as following a link or submitting a form and reloading the page. It does not stop bubbling, because that is the job of stopPropagation.

Common mistake: handling a form submit without calling event.preventDefault(). The page reloads, your DOM changes vanish, and the user's input is lost.

questions.prompt:
A city library's catalogue page has a table with id books. Each row holds a book title and a link with class reserve. Rows are added as the user scrolls, so one click listener (default options) is placed on the table. Trace a user clicking the reserve link inside a cell of row 5.

Step 1: Capturing runs from document down through body, the table, the row and the cell.
Step 2: The event reaches its target, the reserve link.
Step 3: ???
Step 4: The listener calls event.target.closest('a.reserve'), finds the link, calls event.preventDefault() so the browser does not follow the link, and marks row 5 as reserved.

Which statement correctly fills Step 3?
choices: Bubbling starts again at document and moves down to the table, and the table's listener fires.
The event ends at the link, because the link itself has no listener of its own to pass it on.
Bubbling carries the event back up through the cell, the row and the table, and the table's listener fires.
The table's listener already fired during Step 1, because the table is an ancestor the event passed on the way down.
questions.why: Listeners run during bubbling by default, so the event travels back up from the link through each ancestor and reaches the table's listener there.

questions.prompt: A dashboard has a div with id panel. Inside it is a paragraph, and inside that paragraph is a span. A click listener is registered only on the panel. The user clicks directly on the span. Inside the listener, what are event.target and event.currentTarget?
choices: both are the span, because that is where the click started
target is the span; currentTarget is the panel
target is the panel; currentTarget is the span
target is the paragraph; currentTarget is the panel
questions.why: event.target is the innermost element where the event started (the span), and event.currentTarget is the element whose listener is running (the panel).

questions.prompt: A gym's signup page has a form. Its submit listener reads the name field and adds a 'Thanks, Priya!' message to the page. Testers report that the message flashes for a moment, then disappears and the name field is empty again. What is the most likely fix?
choices: Register the listener with { capture: true } so it runs before the page reacts
Call event.preventDefault() in the submit listener so the browser does not submit and reload
Call event.stopPropagation() in the submit listener so the event cannot reach any ancestors
Move the submit listener from the form up to the body element using delegation
questions.why: Without preventDefault the browser performs its built-in submit, reloading the page, which wipes the DOM change and the user's input.

questions.prompt: A shop page shows product cards. Each card has a click listener that opens a quick-view box. Inside one card is a 'Details' link with its own click listener that calls only event.preventDefault(). The user clicks the 'Details' link. What happens?
choices: The link is not followed, and the card's listener still runs and opens the quick-view box.
The link is followed, but the card's listener does not run.
The link is followed, and then the card's listener runs as the event bubbles.
The link is not followed, and the card's listener does not run because preventDefault halted the event.
questions.why: preventDefault cancels only the browser's built-in action (following the link); it does not stop bubbling, so the card's listener still receives the event.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how bubbling makes event delegation possible, and when preventDefault is needed. Name one limit or tradeoff, for example what goes wrong if someone calls stopPropagation or forgets preventDefault.
lessons.modelAnswer: When you click something, the event first travels down from the document to the clicked element, which is capturing. Then it bubbles back up through every ancestor, and normal listeners run during that upward trip. So a single listener on a parent hears clicks from all its children. With event.target, usually combined with closest, it can work out which child was actually hit. That is delegation. It means one listener instead of hundreds, and it also works for items added later. One tradeoff: if some inner code calls stopPropagation, the event never reaches the parent and the delegated handler silently stops working. preventDefault is a separate tool. It cancels the browser's built-in action, such as navigating on a link or reloading the page on a form submit. If you forget it on submit, your updates vanish on reload.
rubricPoints: Events capture down to the target and then bubble back up through its ancestors.
Delegation puts one listener on a parent and uses event.target to identify the child that was clicked.
Delegation also works for children added after the listener was attached.
preventDefault cancels the browser's default action and does not stop bubbling.
A forgotten preventDefault on form submit causes a reload that wipes DOM changes.
stopPropagation can silently break delegated handlers higher up the page.

suggested.rationale: Bubbling order, delegation and preventDefault are best learned by clicking elements in a live page and watching which handlers fire, which the planned JavaScript lab would support.

lessons.plain: A web form is the part of a page where people type information and send it, like a sign-up box or a checkout page. Form validation means checking that what they typed makes sense before you accept it: the email looks like an email, the required boxes are filled, the password is long enough. Think of a receptionist glancing over a paper form before filing it. They catch blanks and obvious typos on the spot, which saves everyone a trip. They cannot prove the details are true, though. That deeper check still happens later, in the back office, which for a website means the server.
lessons.guessPrompt: A user fills in a sign-up form and presses Enter instead of clicking the Submit button. If your JavaScript only listens for a click on the button, do you think your validation code runs? Why or why not?
lessons.teach:
A form is an HTML element that groups input fields and sends their values somewhere when submitted. Submission fires a submit event on the form itself. This happens whether the user clicks a submit button or presses Enter in a field. By default the browser then sends the data and loads a new page.

Validation is checking input before accepting it. Browsers have built-in validation: attributes such as required (must not be empty), type="email" (must look like an address), minlength and pattern (must match a rule). In JavaScript, input.validity describes what is wrong with a field. form.checkValidity() returns true only if every field passes. input.setCustomValidity(message) marks a field invalid with your own message, and an empty string clears it. reportValidity() shows those messages to the user. FormData is an object that collects all named field values from a form in one go.

Worked example: a sign-up form has email and password fields, and you attach a listener to the form's submit event. The user types "bob@" and presses Enter. First, submit fires on the form. Second, your handler calls event.preventDefault(), which stops the browser's page load. Third, it checks the password length and calls setCustomValidity("At least 8 characters") if the password is too short. Fourth, form.reportValidity() returns false and the browser shows the messages. Fifth, the handler returns early. Once the input is fixed, the handler builds new FormData(form) and sends it with fetch, a function that makes a network request from JavaScript.

One common mistake is forgetting preventDefault. The page reloads, your error messages flash and vanish, and the data may be sent unchecked. Another is listening for click on the button, which misses Enter key submissions. Also remember that client-side checks are for convenience only. Anyone can bypass them, so the server must validate again before trusting the data.

questions.prompt: A bakery's online order form has a 'cakes' number field and a 'pickupDate' field. A listener is attached to the form's submit event. A customer enters 30 cakes and presses Enter. Step 1: submit fires on the form. Step 2: the handler calls event.preventDefault() so the browser does not load a new page. Step 3: the handler sees 30 is over the shop's limit of 24 and calls cakesInput.setCustomValidity('Maximum 24 cakes per order'). (When the number is 24 or less, it calls setCustomValidity('') instead.) Step 4: MISSING. This step must both show the error messages to the customer and return false because a field is invalid. Step 5: because the result was false, the handler returns early. After the customer fixes the number, the handler builds new FormData(form) and sends it with fetch. Which call belongs in Step 4?
choices: form.reportValidity(), which returns false and displays the messages to the customer
cakesInput.validity, which describes what is wrong with the cakes field
form.checkValidity(), which returns false because the cakes field is marked invalid
new FormData(form), which collects the field values so they can be checked
questions.why: reportValidity() is the call that both returns whether every field passes and shows the validation messages to the user, while checkValidity() only returns true or false without showing anything.

questions.prompt: On a hotel booking form, your code called guestsInput.setCustomValidity('No more than 6 guests per room') when a visitor typed 9. The visitor changes the value to 4. What should your code do to the guests field now so the form can be submitted?
choices: Call form.checkValidity() to remove the custom error message
Call guestsInput.setCustomValidity('') to clear the custom error
Call guestsInput.setCustomValidity('Valid') to mark it as passing
Call event.preventDefault() so the old message is discarded
questions.why: Passing an empty string to setCustomValidity clears the custom error; any non-empty message, even 'Valid', keeps the field marked invalid.

questions.prompt: A developer validates a newsletter sign-up form by attaching a listener to the click event of its Subscribe button, not to the form. A visitor types an address into the email field and presses Enter. What happens?
choices: The click handler runs because pressing Enter counts as a click on any element in the form
FormData automatically runs the click handler before sending the field values
The browser blocks the submission because no submit listener is attached to the form
The form is submitted without the click handler running, so its checks are skipped
questions.why: Pressing Enter in a field fires submit on the form without a button click, so a click listener on the button misses that submission and its validation never runs.

questions.prompt: A gym's membership form uses required, type="email" and a JavaScript length check before sending data with fetch. The team says the server can now store submissions without checking them again. Why is this unsafe?
choices: The required attribute is ignored whenever the form is sent with fetch
reportValidity() only works on the server, so the browser checks never run
Client-side checks are only a convenience and anyone can bypass them, so the server must validate the data again
Browsers only run built-in validation on forms that also have a click listener
questions.why: Checks in the browser can be bypassed by anyone, so they only help honest users, and the server must re-validate before trusting the data.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would validate a sign-up form in vanilla JavaScript, which event you hook into and why, and name one limit of doing validation in the browser.
lessons.modelAnswer: I attach one listener to the form's submit event, not to the button's click, because submit fires for both a button click and an Enter keypress. The first thing the handler does is call event.preventDefault(), so the browser does not reload the page before my code finishes. I lean on built-in attributes like required, type="email" and minlength. For rules HTML can't express, I use setCustomValidity on the specific field, then call form.reportValidity() so the user sees the messages. If that returns false, I stop. If it passes, I collect values with new FormData(form) and send them with fetch. The limit is that browser validation is only a convenience. Anyone can switch off JavaScript or send a request directly, so the server has to repeat every check. The client check just gives faster feedback and saves pointless requests.
rubricPoints: Listens for the form's submit event rather than a button click, so Enter submissions are caught.
Calls preventDefault to stop the default page reload.
Uses built-in constraints and/or setCustomValidity with checkValidity or reportValidity.
Gathers values, for example with FormData, only after validation passes.
States that client-side validation can be bypassed, so the server must validate too.

suggested.rationale: Validating a form well comes from actually wiring a submit handler and watching what happens with and without preventDefault, which a JavaScript lab would let the learner do.

lessons.plain: Accessibility means building pages that everyone can use, including people who navigate with only a keyboard or who rely on a screen reader, a program that reads the page aloud. When JavaScript changes a page, it can quietly break this: a new message appears that the screen reader never mentions, or a clickable box can't be reached with the Tab key. Think of a shop that rearranges its shelves overnight. Sighted shoppers adapt instantly, but someone shopping by touch needs to be told what moved. Accessible DOM code does that telling.
lessons.guessPrompt: A page has a 'Show details' control built from a plain div with a click listener attached. A user who cannot use a mouse presses Tab to try to reach it. What do you think happens, and why?
lessons.teach:
Accessibility (often shortened to a11y) is making a page usable by people with disabilities. The browser builds an accessibility tree, a simplified copy of the DOM that assistive technology such as a screen reader reads aloud. When your JavaScript manipulates the DOM, you must keep that tree accurate.

Four basic habits cover most cases. First, use semantic elements, meaning HTML tags whose names describe their role: button for actions, a for links, label for form fields. A real button is focusable (it can receive keyboard focus via Tab), activates on Enter and Space, and is announced as a button, all for free. Second, report state with ARIA attributes, extra attributes that describe meaning to assistive technology; aria-expanded="true" or "false" tells a listener whether a collapsible panel is open. Third, announce dynamic content with a live region, an element marked aria-live="polite" whose text changes are read out when the user is idle. Fourth, manage focus: when you open a dialog, move focus into it, and when you close it, return focus to the control that opened it.

Worked example, a menu toggle. Step 1: the markup is a button with aria-expanded="false" and a hidden menu. Step 2: the user tabs to the button and presses Enter, which fires its click listener. Step 3: the listener shows the menu and sets aria-expanded to "true". Step 4: the screen reader announces the button as expanded. Step 5: a status message such as 'Item added' is written into an existing live region, so it is spoken aloud.

A common mistake is attaching a click listener to a div and styling it to look like a button. It is not focusable, ignores the Enter key and is announced as plain text. The consequence in a running site is that keyboard and screen-reader users simply cannot use that feature, even though it looks fine to everyone testing with a mouse.

questions.prompt: A bakery's website has a 'View order #482' button. Clicking it opens a dialog showing that order's details. The developer handles accessibility like this. Step 1: the user tabs to 'View order #482' and presses Enter, which fires its click listener. Step 2: the listener shows the dialog and moves keyboard focus to the dialog's Close button. Step 3: the user reads the order and activates Close, and the listener hides the dialog. Step 4: ??? Which action belongs in Step 4?
choices: Leave focus on the Close button, since that was the last control the user used
Move focus to the top of the page so the user starts again from the beginning
Set aria-live="polite" on the hidden dialog so its closing is announced
Return focus to the 'View order #482' button that opened the dialog
questions.why: When a dialog closes, focus should go back to the control that opened it, so keyboard and screen-reader users continue from where they were.

questions.prompt: A shoe store's page shows a basket count. When a shopper adds a pair, JavaScript updates the count to '3 items in basket'. Sighted users notice the change, but screen-reader users hear nothing. What is the best basic fix?
choices: Change the count's text colour so it stands out after each update
Attach a click listener to the basket count so users can request it
Write the new message into an existing element marked aria-live="polite"
Add aria-expanded="true" to the basket count element
questions.why: A live region marked aria-live="polite" has its text changes read aloud when the user is idle, so dynamic updates get announced.

questions.prompt: On a recipe site, a developer makes a 'Save recipe' control from a span element, styles it like a button and attaches a click listener. It works perfectly when tested with a mouse. What happens for other users?
choices: Screen readers announce it as a button because the styling makes it look like one
It works for keyboard users but is skipped by screen readers
Keyboard users cannot Tab to it or activate it with Enter, and screen readers announce it as plain text
Nothing changes, because the click listener also responds to the Enter key
questions.why: Only a real semantic button gets focusability, Enter and Space activation, and the button role for free. A styled span gets none of these.

questions.prompt: A job board has a 'Show filters' button with aria-expanded="false". Its click listener reveals the filter panel but does not change any attributes. What does a screen-reader user hear after pressing the button, and what fixes it?
choices: The panel contents are read automatically, so no fix is needed
The button is announced as a link; it should be changed to an a element
The button is still announced as collapsed; the listener should set aria-expanded to "true"
Nothing is announced; the button should be replaced with a div
questions.why: aria-expanded reports the open or closed state to assistive technology, so it must be updated whenever the panel is shown or hidden.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why you'd replace their clickable div with a button and add aria-expanded and a live region to their collapsible panel, and name one limit of these fixes.
lessons.modelAnswer: Screen readers and keyboard users don't see our page; they work from the accessibility tree the browser builds from the DOM. A div with a click listener isn't focusable, doesn't respond to Enter or Space, and is announced as plain text, so keyboard users can't trigger it. A real button gives us focus, keyboard activation and the right announcement for free. Because our script opens and closes the panel, we also update aria-expanded so listeners know its current state, and we put status messages into an aria-live region so changes are actually spoken. When a dialog opens, we move focus into it and return it afterwards. The limit is that ARIA only describes things; it adds no behaviour. Putting role or aria attributes on a div doesn't make it keyboard-operable, and wrong ARIA can mislead users more than none at all.
rubricPoints: Assistive technology reads an accessibility tree derived from the DOM, so DOM changes must keep it accurate.
Semantic elements like button give focus, keyboard activation and correct announcement automatically.
ARIA attributes such as aria-expanded communicate state that JavaScript changes.
Live regions make dynamic messages get announced.
Focus should be moved deliberately when content like a dialog opens or closes.
ARIA describes meaning but adds no behaviour, which is a key limit.

suggested.rationale: A JavaScript lab that lets learners convert a div-based widget into an accessible button with aria-expanded and a live region, then check keyboard behaviour, builds the habit better than reading alone.

lessons.plain: JavaScript runs your code on a single thread, meaning it can only do one thing at a time. The call stack is its list of what it is doing right now. Slow jobs like timers or network requests are handed off to the surrounding environment (the browser or Node.js), and when they finish, their follow-up work waits in a line called the task queue. The event loop is the doorman: whenever the stack is empty, it lets the next waiting task in. Picture a lone chef who cooks one dish at a time while helpers watch the ovens and pin finished orders to a board.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a program logs "A", then sets a timer for 0 milliseconds that logs "B", then logs "C", in what order do you think the three letters appear, and why?
lessons.teach:
The call stack is the record of which functions are currently running. Calling a function pushes it onto the stack, and returning pops it off. JavaScript has one stack, so only one piece of your code runs at any moment.

The host environment is the program running JavaScript, such as a browser or Node.js. It provides slow operations like timers and network requests and does that waiting outside your code. When an operation finishes, the host places its callback, the function you asked it to run afterwards, into the task queue. The task queue is a first-in, first-out waiting line. The event loop is a repeating check: if the call stack is empty, it takes the next task from the queue and runs it. A related line, the microtask queue, holds promise follow-ups and is emptied completely before the next task is taken. The key rule is that nothing from either queue interrupts code that is already running.

Worked example: console.log("A"); setTimeout(() => console.log("B"), 0); console.log("C");
Step 1: log "A" runs on the stack and prints A.
Step 2: setTimeout hands the timer to the host and returns immediately.
Step 3: the timer expires almost at once, so the host puts the callback that logs "B" in the task queue.
Step 4: log "C" runs and prints C. The script finishes and the stack empties.
Step 5: the event loop sees an empty stack, takes the callback and prints B.
The output is A, C, B.

A common mistake is believing that a 0 ms timer runs immediately. The delay is only a minimum. The callback still waits until the stack is empty. In a running system, a long synchronous loop keeps the stack busy. While it runs, a browser page freezes and stops responding to clicks, and a Node.js server cannot answer any other request. Every queued callback, including timers, runs late.

questions.prompt:
A bakery's inventory script runs this code: console.log("open"); setTimeout(() => console.log("restock"), 0); Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log("count")); console.log("close");
Step 1: log "open" runs on the call stack and prints open.
Step 2: setTimeout hands the timer to the host and returns at once. Soon after, the host puts the restock callback in the task queue.
Step 3: the promise follow-up that logs "count" is placed in the microtask queue.
Step 4: log "close" runs and prints close. The script finishes and the call stack is empty.
Step 5: ???
Step 6: the event loop takes the restock callback from the task queue and prints restock.
Final output: open, close, count, restock. Which choice correctly fills in Step 5?
choices: Before any task is taken, the microtask queue is emptied completely, so the count follow-up runs and prints count.
The host runs count and restock at the same moment on two separate call stacks.
The event loop takes the restock callback first, because it was queued before the promise follow-up.
The count follow-up already printed partway through Step 4, because promise follow-ups interrupt running code.
questions.why: The microtask queue, which holds promise follow-ups, is emptied completely before the event loop takes the next task, so count prints before restock but only after the running script finishes.

questions.prompt: In JavaScript's conceptual model, what is the job of the event loop?
choices: It pauses the currently running function whenever a timer expires so the timer's callback can run on time.
It repeatedly checks whether the call stack is empty and, if so, takes the next waiting task from the queue and runs it.
It keeps a record of which functions are currently running, pushing on each call and popping on each return.
It performs slow operations such as network requests itself, inside your code, while other functions wait.
questions.why: The event loop is a repeating check that moves the next task onto the stack only when the stack is empty. The record of running functions is the call stack, and slow operations are handled by the host.

questions.prompt: A weather dashboard runs: setTimeout(() => console.log("rain"), 0); setTimeout(() => console.log("wind"), 0); console.log("loaded"); What is printed, in order?
choices: rain, wind, loaded
rain, loaded, wind
loaded, wind, rain
loaded, rain, wind
questions.why: loaded prints first because synchronous code finishes before any queued callback runs. The task queue is first-in, first-out, so rain, which was queued first, runs before wind.

questions.prompt: A Node.js server receives a request that starts a synchronous loop taking 4 seconds to build a report. At 1 second, a second user sends a request, and a 200 ms timer set at the start has already expired. What happens?
choices: The second request is answered at 1 second because the host handles requests outside your code.
The timer callback is dropped because its 200 ms delay passed while the stack was busy.
Neither the timer callback nor the second request is handled until the 4-second loop finishes and the stack empties.
The timer callback interrupts the loop at 200 ms, and the second request is answered right after it.
questions.why: Nothing from the queues interrupts code that is already running. A long synchronous loop keeps the stack busy, so the server cannot answer other requests and every queued callback, including the timer, runs late rather than being dropped.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, how the call stack, task queue and event loop work together while a program waits for a timer or network call, and name one limit of this single-threaded model.
lessons.modelAnswer: JavaScript has one call stack, so it runs one piece of code at a time. When we start something slow, like a timer or a fetch, the browser or Node takes over the waiting, and our code carries on. When that slow work finishes, its callback goes into the task queue. The event loop keeps checking whether the stack is empty. When it is, the loop pulls the next callback from the queue and runs it. Promise follow-ups sit in a separate microtask queue, and that queue is drained first. So waiting does not block us. However, queued work can only start once the current code finishes. That is the limit. A long synchronous loop or heavy calculation freezes the page or stalls the server for every user, and a 0 ms timer does not mean immediately. It only means as soon as the stack is free.
rubricPoints: The call stack holds the currently running functions, and there is only one, so code runs one thing at a time.
The host environment, the browser or Node.js, does the actual waiting for timers and network calls.
Finished callbacks wait in the task queue, and promise follow-ups wait in a microtask queue that is drained first.
The event loop moves queued work onto the stack only when the stack is empty.
Long synchronous work blocks everything, so callbacks and timers run late and the page or server becomes unresponsive.

suggested.rationale: Predicting and then watching the stack and queues step through real snippets in a JavaScript lab builds this mental model better than reading alone.

lessons.plain: A callback is a function you hand to another function so it can call you back when a slow job, like downloading data, is finished. It is like leaving your phone number at a restaurant: you do not stand at the door waiting, and they ring you when a table is free. The trouble starts when each step needs the result of the one before. You end up nesting one callback inside another, and the code drifts sideways into a pyramid that is hard to read and easy to break. People call this callback hell, and it is the mess that async/await was designed to clean up.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose you must load a user, then that user's orders, then the first order's shipping status, and each load takes time and gives its result to a function you pass in. If you write each next step inside the previous step's function, what do you think the code will look like after three steps, and where would you have to check for errors?
lessons.teach:
A callback is a function passed as an argument to another function, to be run later. Asynchronous code is code that starts a slow task, such as a network request or file read, and lets the program keep running instead of freezing until the task ends. Before newer tools existed, callbacks were the main way JavaScript said "run this when the slow thing is done."

Many libraries use the error-first callback convention: the callback receives an error as its first argument (empty if all went well) and the result as its second. This lets one function handle both success and failure.

Worked example. We need three dependent steps. First, getUser(id, callback) runs; when it finishes it calls our function with (err, user). Inside that function we check err, then call getOrders(user.id, callback2). When that finishes, callback2 receives (err, orders); we check err again and call getShipping(orders[0].id, callback3). Finally callback3 receives (err, status), we check err a third time and print status. Each step lives inside the previous one, so the code indents further right with every call. That rightward pyramid of nested callbacks, with error checks repeated at every level, is callback hell.

Why it hurts: the order of steps is buried in nesting, every level needs its own error check, and you cannot use an ordinary try/catch around the whole thing because the callbacks run later, after the surrounding code has already finished.

A common mistake is forgetting to stop after handling an error, for example logging err but not returning, so the code goes on to read user.id from an undefined user and crashes. Another is calling the callback twice. In a running server, this shows up as crashes, requests that never get answered, or a response sent twice.

async/await keeps the same dependent steps but lets you write them top to bottom, like normal code, with one try/catch covering all of them.

questions.prompt: A city library app looks up a member's overdue fines with error-first callbacks (the callback gets an error first, empty if all went well, then the result). Step 1: findMember(cardNumber, cb) finishes and calls cb with (err, member). Step 2: inside cb, if err is set, log it and then ______. Step 3: otherwise call findLoans(member.memberId, cb2). Step 4: cb2 receives (err, loans); check err the same way, then call sumFines(loans, cb3). Step 5: cb3 receives (err, total); check err a final time and display total. What belongs in the blank in Step 2?
choices: call cb a second time with the error so the caller hears about it
return right away, so findLoans is never called with an undefined member
rely on a try/catch placed around the findMember call to stop the chain
carry on to Step 3, because only the last callback needs to stop on an error
questions.why: If the code logs the error but does not return, it goes on to read member.memberId from an undefined member and crashes, so it must stop right after handling the error.

questions.prompt: A weather library uses the error-first callback convention and calls your function as handler(err, forecast). The request for tomorrow's forecast succeeds. What do the two arguments hold?
choices: err holds a success message, and forecast holds the result
err holds the result, and forecast is empty
err is empty, and forecast holds the result
both arguments hold the same forecast object
questions.why: In the error-first convention the first argument is the error, left empty when all went well, and the second argument is the result.

questions.prompt: A photo-sharing site resizes an image, uploads it, then saves a database record, using three nested callbacks. A developer wraps the whole block in one ordinary try/catch, but when the database step fails, the catch block never runs. Why?
choices: The callbacks run later, after the code around the try/catch has already finished
try/catch only catches errors from the first callback in a chain
The error-first convention turns every error into a plain string that try/catch ignores
Nested callbacks always swallow errors, so nothing could ever report the failure
questions.why: Callbacks run after the slow task ends, by which time the surrounding try/catch code has already finished, so an ordinary try/catch cannot cover them.

questions.prompt: A concert-ticket service checks seat availability, then reserves the seat, then charges the card, then emails a receipt. Each step needs the result of the one before. Today this is written as four nested callbacks. What does rewriting it with async/await give you?
choices: The four steps run at the same time, so the purchase finishes faster
Errors can no longer happen, so the error checks can simply be deleted
The program freezes on each step, so no other code can run while it waits
The same dependent steps, written top to bottom, with one try/catch around all of them
questions.why: async/await keeps the same dependent order but lets you write the steps top to bottom like normal code, with a single try/catch covering every step.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, what a callback is, why chaining dependent callbacks turns into callback hell, and what async/await gives you instead. Name at least one limit or tradeoff of plain callbacks.
lessons.modelAnswer: A callback is just a function you pass to another function so it gets run later, usually when something slow like a network call finishes. That lets the program keep working instead of freezing. The problem comes when steps depend on each other: to get orders you need the user, and to get shipping you need the order, so each call has to go inside the previous callback. The code nests deeper and drifts right, and you must check for an error at every level. A tradeoff is that you cannot wrap the whole sequence in one try/catch, because the callbacks run after that code has already finished, and it is easy to forget to return after an error or to call a callback twice, which in a server means crashes or hung requests. async/await lets you write the same dependent steps top to bottom with one try/catch around them.
rubricPoints: Defines a callback as a function passed in to be run later when a task finishes.
Explains that dependent asynchronous steps force nesting, producing the rightward pyramid called callback hell.
Notes that error handling must be repeated at each level and a single try/catch cannot wrap callbacks that run later.
Names a concrete risk such as forgetting to return after an error or calling a callback twice.
States that async/await expresses the same dependent sequence top to bottom with one try/catch.

suggested.rationale: Writing a three-step nested callback chain, breaking it with a missed error return, and then rewriting it with async/await in a JavaScript lab makes the pain and the fix concrete in a way reading cannot.
