lessons.plain: A promise is a placeholder for a result that is not ready yet, such as data coming back from a server. Think of the buzzer a busy café hands you when you order. Right now it is just a buzzer, but later it will either light up because your food is ready or flash an error because the kitchen ran out. You can decide in advance what to do in each case and carry on with other things. A promise lets a program keep working while slow jobs finish, then react when they succeed or fail.
lessons.guessPrompt: You order three dishes and get one buzzer that goes off only when all three are ready. If the kitchen burns one dish, what should that single buzzer tell you, and should you still wait for the other two?
lessons.teach:
A promise is a JavaScript object that represents the eventual result of an asynchronous operation, meaning work that finishes later, such as a network request. Every promise is in exactly one of three states. Pending means not finished yet. Fulfilled means it succeeded and holds a value. Rejected means it failed and holds a reason, usually an Error. Once a promise is fulfilled or rejected it is called settled, and it never changes state again.

You react to a promise by attaching callbacks, which are functions JavaScript runs for you later. The .then method takes a function that runs with the value on success. The .catch method takes a function that runs with the reason on failure. The .finally method runs a function either way, which is handy for cleanup like hiding a loading spinner. Each of these returns a new promise, so you can chain them. Whatever a .then callback returns becomes the value passed to the next .then. If any step throws or rejects, the chain skips ahead to the nearest .catch.

Promise.all takes a list of promises and returns one promise. It fulfills with an array of all the values, in the original order, once every input has fulfilled. It rejects as soon as any one input rejects.

Worked example: getUser() takes 1 second and getOrders() takes 2 seconds. Promise.all([getUser(), getOrders()]) starts both at once. At 1 second the user arrives and the combined promise stays pending. At 2 seconds the orders arrive and the combined promise fulfills with [user, orders]. Total wait is about 2 seconds, not 3. If getOrders had rejected instead, the combined promise would reject and .catch would run. If you want every outcome regardless of failures, a related method, Promise.allSettled, waits for all of them.

A common mistake is forgetting to return a promise inside .then. The next step then runs immediately with undefined instead of waiting. In a running app this causes missing data, and errors that escape every .catch, which can show up as unhandled rejection warnings or crashes.

questions.prompt: A library website needs three things before it can draw its home page: getBooks() takes 2 seconds, getAuthors() takes 5 seconds, and getReviews() takes 3 seconds. The code is Promise.all([getBooks(), getAuthors(), getReviews()]).then(showPage).catch(showError). Here is the trace. Step 1: at 0 seconds, all three requests start at the same time. Step 2: at 2 seconds the books arrive, and the combined promise stays pending. Step 3: at 3 seconds the reviews arrive, and the combined promise is still pending. Step 4: at 5 seconds the authors arrive. What happens at Step 4?
choices: The combined promise fulfills with [books, reviews, authors], which is the order the results arrived in, and showPage runs after about 10 seconds in total.
The combined promise stays pending because each input promise has to be passed to its own .then before Promise.all can finish.
The combined promise fulfills with [books, authors, reviews], which is the original order, and showPage runs after about 5 seconds in total.
The combined promise fulfills with only the authors, because that was the last value to arrive, and showError runs for the other two.
questions.why: Promise.all fulfills only once every input has fulfilled, which happens at 5 seconds here because the slowest request takes 5 seconds, and the values come back in the order the promises were listed, not the order they arrived.

questions.prompt: A photo-sharing app starts an upload and gets back a promise. The upload fails, and the promise rejects with an Error saying "file too large". Which statement about that promise is true?
choices: It goes back to pending so that the upload can be retried automatically.
It can still become fulfilled later if the same upload succeeds on a second try.
It is still pending until a .catch callback is attached to it.
It is settled in the rejected state, and it will never change to fulfilled or back to pending.
questions.why: Once a promise is fulfilled or rejected it is settled, and a settled promise never changes state again.

questions.prompt: A weather dashboard runs Promise.all([getForecast(), getAlerts(), getRadar()]).then(draw).catch(warn). getForecast fulfills after 4 seconds. getAlerts rejects after 1 second. getRadar fulfills after 3 seconds. What happens?
choices: After 4 seconds the combined promise fulfills with [forecast, radar], and the failed alert is left out.
After 1 second the combined promise fulfills with [forecast, undefined, radar], and draw runs.
After about 1 second the combined promise rejects, and warn runs.
After 4 seconds the combined promise rejects, because Promise.all waits for every input before it reports a failure.
questions.why: Promise.all rejects as soon as any one input rejects, so the rejection of getAlerts at 1 second makes the combined promise reject at once, and the chain skips to .catch.

questions.prompt: A fitness app has this chain: fetchWorkout().then(w => { saveToCache(w); }).then(result => showSaved(result)). The function saveToCache returns a promise that takes 2 seconds to finish. What actually happens?
choices: The second .then runs immediately with undefined, and if saveToCache fails, that error is not handled by this chain.
showSaved receives the workout w, because each .then passes its own input along to the next .then automatically.
The second .then waits 2 seconds for saveToCache, and then showSaved receives the cached workout.
The chain stops after the first .then, because a callback must return a value before the chain can continue.
questions.why: The first callback does not return the promise from saveToCache, so it returns undefined, and the next step runs right away instead of waiting; any failure inside saveToCache also escapes the chain and can appear as an unhandled rejection.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a promise is, what its three states mean, how .then, .catch and .finally fit together, and when you would use Promise.all. Name one limit or tradeoff of Promise.all.
lessons.modelAnswer: A promise is an object that stands in for a result that isn't ready yet. It starts pending, then settles once, either fulfilled with a value or rejected with an error, and never changes after that. We attach .then to handle the value, .catch to handle a failure anywhere earlier in the chain, and .finally for cleanup that should run either way. Each returns a new promise, so steps chain, but you must return inside .then or the next step won't wait. Promise.all runs several independent promises at the same time and gives back their values in order, so total time is roughly the slowest one rather than the sum. The tradeoff is that it fails fast: if any one rejects, the whole thing rejects and you lose the successful results, so for partial success you'd use Promise.allSettled.
rubricPoints: Defines a promise as a placeholder for a future result of asynchronous work.
Names pending, fulfilled and rejected, and notes a settled promise never changes.
Explains .then for success, .catch for failure, .finally for either, and that they chain.
Describes Promise.all running promises together and returning values in order.
States that Promise.all rejects as soon as any input rejects.
Mentions the risk of forgetting to return a promise inside .then.

suggested.rationale: Seeing promise states change and Promise.all fail fast is best learned by running and timing real promises in a JavaScript lab, which no current mission provides.

lessons.plain: Some work in a program takes time, like asking a server for data. JavaScript represents that waiting with a promise: an object meaning 'a result will arrive later, or a failure will.' The async and await keywords let you write that waiting code so it reads top to bottom, like ordinary steps in a recipe. When a step fails, you catch the problem with try/catch, the same way you would catch any other error. Think of a cook following a recipe: wait for the oven to heat, then bake. If the oven breaks, the cook stops at that step and switches to a backup plan.
lessons.guessPrompt: A function does three steps in order: get a user, then get that user's latest order, then show the order. Each step must wait for the one before it. If the second step fails because the server is down, what do you think should happen to the third step, and where would you want the program to go instead?
lessons.teach:
An async function is a function marked with the async keyword. It always returns a promise, which is an object standing for a value that will exist later (resolved) or a failure (rejected). Inside an async function, await pauses that function until a promise settles. If the promise resolves, await hands back its value. If it rejects, await throws the error at that line, just like a normal throw. That is why try/catch works: the try block holds the steps, and the catch block runs if any awaited step throws. An optional finally block runs either way, which is useful for cleanup such as hiding a loading spinner.

Worked example: async function loadOrder(id) { try { const user = await getUser(id); const order = await getOrder(user.lastOrderId); return order; } catch (err) { console.log('Could not load:', err.message); return null; } }

Trace it. First, getUser(id) returns a promise; await pauses loadOrder. Second, the promise resolves with a user object, so user holds real data. Third, getOrder runs with user.lastOrderId and loadOrder pauses again. Suppose that request rejects. Fourth, await throws, the return line is skipped, and control jumps to catch, which logs the message and returns null. Whoever called loadOrder receives a promise that resolves to null instead of failing.

Common mistake: forgetting await. Writing const user = getUser(id) stores the promise itself, not the user, so user.lastOrderId is undefined. Worse, if that promise later rejects, the error never passes through your try block, so catch cannot see it.

In a running system, an uncaught rejection becomes an unhandled promise rejection. In a browser that means a silent failure, and in Node.js it can stop the whole process. Awaiting every promise inside try/catch keeps failures contained and gives you one clear place to decide what happens next.

questions.prompt: A weather app uses this function: async function showForecast(city) { try { const place = await findPlace(city); const days = await fetchForecast(place.stationId); drawChart(days); } catch (err) { showBanner('Forecast unavailable: ' + err.message); } finally { hideSpinner(); } }. Trace a call to showForecast('Oslo'). Step 1: findPlace('Oslo') returns a promise and await pauses showForecast. Step 2: that promise resolves, so place holds a real object with stationId 7. Step 3: fetchForecast(7) runs and showForecast pauses again, but this request rejects with a timeout error. Step 4: ??? Step 5: the finally block runs hideSpinner(), and the promise returned by showForecast resolves instead of failing. Which choice correctly fills in Step 4?
choices: The finally block runs first to hide the spinner, then control returns to the try block to retry fetchForecast(7).
await hands back undefined, so days is undefined and drawChart(undefined) runs before the catch block is checked.
The rejection is ignored inside the function, drawChart is skipped, and the error is passed straight to whoever called showForecast.
await throws the error at the fetchForecast line, drawChart(days) is skipped, and control jumps to catch, which shows the banner.
questions.why: When an awaited promise rejects, await throws at that line just like a normal throw, so the remaining try steps are skipped and the catch block handles the error before finally runs.

questions.prompt: A bakery's ordering site has a function declared as async function countCakes() { return 12; }. It contains no await at all. What does calling countCakes() give the caller?
choices: The number 12 directly, because there is nothing to wait for.
An error, because the async keyword is only allowed on functions that use await.
undefined, because an async function without await never returns a value.
A promise that resolves to 12, because an async function always returns a promise.
questions.why: An async function always returns a promise, so the returned 12 is wrapped in a promise that resolves to 12.

questions.prompt: A payroll tool has: async function loadPayslip(staffId) { try { const staff = getStaff(staffId); const slip = await getPayslip(staff.payrollCode); return slip; } catch (err) { return null; } }. The developer notices getPayslip is always called with undefined. What is the cause?
choices: getPayslip must also be called without await so both lines match.
try/catch blocks automatically clear any variables declared inside them.
getStaff(staffId) is missing await, so staff holds a promise, not the staff object, and staff.payrollCode is undefined.
The catch block runs too early and replaces staff with null.
questions.why: Without await, staff stores the promise itself, and a promise has no payrollCode property, so undefined is passed on; a later rejection of that promise would also escape the catch block.

questions.prompt: A library app runs this in Node.js: async function listLoans(memberId) { const member = await getMember(memberId); const loans = await getLoans(member.cardNumber); return loans; }. There is no try/catch anywhere, and nothing that calls listLoans handles errors either. If getLoans rejects, what is the likely result for the running system?
choices: await keeps pausing forever, so the request hangs but the process stays healthy.
listLoans quietly returns an empty list, because await turns rejections into empty values.
An unhandled promise rejection, which in Node.js can stop the whole process.
The error is logged and the function returns null, the same as if a catch block were present.
questions.why: Without try/catch the thrown error escapes as an uncaught rejection, which in Node.js can stop the whole process; wrapping the awaited steps in try/catch would contain it.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how async/await and try/catch work together when you make two dependent server calls, and name one limit or pitfall they should watch out for.
lessons.modelAnswer: Marking a function async lets me use await inside it, and the function itself always returns a promise. Each await pauses only that function until the promise settles. If it resolves, I get the value back and move to the next line, so the second call can use data from the first. If it rejects, await throws right there, and the try block hands control to catch, skipping the remaining steps. In catch I log the error and return a fallback, and in finally I do any cleanup. One pitfall is forgetting await: then I'm holding a promise instead of data, and its rejection escapes my try/catch, which in Node can crash the process. Another tradeoff is that awaiting calls one after another runs them in order. That is right for dependent calls, but it is slower if the calls don't actually depend on each other.
rubricPoints: An async function always returns a promise.
await pauses that function until the promise settles and gives back the resolved value.
A rejected promise makes await throw, so try/catch handles it like a normal error.
After a failure, the remaining steps in try are skipped and catch runs; finally runs either way.
Forgetting await lets a rejection escape try/catch and can cause unhandled rejections.
Sequential awaits run the calls in order, which suits dependent calls but is slower for independent ones.

suggested.rationale: Writing and running dependent async calls that sometimes reject, then watching where control goes, is best learned hands-on in a JavaScript lab.

lessons.plain: Fetching data means asking another computer, usually a web server, for information and waiting for its reply. In JavaScript the built-in tool for this is called the Fetch API. The reply often arrives as JSON, which is plain text written in a format that looks like JavaScript objects and lists, so a program can turn it back into real data it can use. Think of ordering by mail. You send a request, a parcel arrives later, and you still have to open the box and check that what came back is what you ordered.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you ask a server for a page that does not exist and it replies with a 404 'Not Found' status, do you think JavaScript's fetch treats that as a failure that throws an error, or as a successful reply that happens to carry bad news? Why?
lessons.teach:
The Fetch API is a function built into browsers and modern Node.js. You call fetch(url) to send an HTTP request, which is a message asking a server for something. fetch does not hand you the data immediately. It returns a promise, which is an object standing in for a result that will arrive later. That promise resolves, meaning it finishes successfully, with a Response object. The Response describes the server's reply. Its status is a number such as 200 for OK or 404 for not found. Its ok property is true only when the status is between 200 and 299.

The body of the reply, the actual content, is not read yet at this point. Calling response.json() reads the body and parses it, which means converting JSON text into real JavaScript objects and arrays. That step takes time too, so json() also returns a promise. Reading data with fetch therefore always takes two waits: one for the response and one for the parsed body.

Here is a worked example. Suppose you write const res = await fetch('/api/users/7'). First, the request goes out. Second, the server answers with status 200 and the text {"id":7,"name":"Ana"}. Third, res.ok is true. Fourth, you write const user = await res.json(), and the text becomes an object. Fifth, user.name gives 'Ana'.

A common mistake is assuming fetch fails whenever something goes wrong. It only rejects on network-level failures, such as no connection or a blocked request. A 404 or 500 status still resolves normally. If you skip checking res.ok, your code calls json() on an error page. That either throws a confusing parsing error or quietly feeds bad data onward.

The consequence in a running app is that real failures show up as blank screens or 'undefined' values instead of clear messages. Check res.ok and throw your own error when it is false. Also note that a body can be read only once, so call json() a single time and keep the result.

questions.prompt: A city library's app loads one book with const res = await fetch('/api/books/315'). Here is how the code runs. Step 1: the request goes out. Step 2: the server is overloaded and replies with status 503 and an HTML error page instead of JSON. Step 3: missing. Step 4: the surrounding try/catch shows the message 'Could not load book (503)' instead of a blank page. Which choice correctly fills in Step 3?
choices: The code calls await res.json() and reads book.title, which comes back as undefined.
The code checks whether res.status is 404, sees that it is not, and goes on to parse the body.
fetch rejects on its own because 503 means something went wrong, so control jumps straight to the catch block.
The code checks res.ok, sees it is false because 503 is outside 200–299, and throws its own error.
questions.why: fetch still resolves on a 503 status, so the app only reaches its catch block with a clear message if it checks res.ok itself and throws when ok is false.

questions.prompt: A fitness tracker runs const res = await fetch('/api/workouts'). When that line finishes, what does res hold?
choices: The raw JSON text of the body as a string
An array of workout objects, already converted from JSON text
A promise that will later resolve to the workout data
A Response object describing the reply, with its body not yet read
questions.why: Awaiting fetch gives you a Response object with properties like status and ok. Turning the body into data takes a separate, second wait.

questions.prompt: A shop's checkout page contains this code: const res = await fetch('/api/cart/88'); const cart = res.json(); console.log(cart.total). The server replies with status 200 and valid JSON that includes a total of 54. What is logged, and why?
choices: 54, because res.ok is true and the JSON is valid
54, because json() converts the text into an object right away
A parsing error, because the body was read twice
undefined, because json() returns a promise that was not awaited, so cart is a promise
questions.why: json() returns a promise, so without await the variable cart is a promise rather than the parsed object, and a promise has no total property.

questions.prompt: A travel site fetches '/api/flights/LX40'. It gets status 200, runs console.log(await res.json()) for debugging, and then on the next line runs const flight = await res.json(). What happens on that second json() call?
choices: It returns the same flight object again, because the result is cached
It sends a fresh request to the server and parses the new reply
It returns the original JSON text, because the body was already parsed
It fails, because a response body can be read only once and it was already read
questions.why: A response body can be read only once, so you should call json() a single time and keep the result in a variable.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, the steps for getting JSON data from a server with fetch. Include at least one limit or trap in how fetch reports errors.
lessons.modelAnswer:
You call fetch with a URL, and it gives back a promise. When that settles, you get a Response object. It tells you the HTTP status and whether ok is true, which means a status in the 200s. The data itself isn't ready yet. You call response.json(), which is also a promise, to read the body and turn the JSON text into real objects. So there are two waits.

The big trap is that fetch only rejects when the request can't complete at all, like a dropped connection. A 404 or 500 counts as a successful fetch. So you have to check response.ok yourself and throw an error if it's false. Otherwise you end up parsing an error page. Two other limits: json() throws if the body isn't valid JSON, and you can only read the body once.
rubricPoints: fetch(url) returns a promise that resolves to a Response object.
The Response carries a status code and an ok flag that is true for 200-299.
response.json() is a second asynchronous step that parses the body text into JavaScript data.
fetch does not reject on HTTP error statuses like 404 or 500, so ok must be checked manually.
Parsing fails if the body is not valid JSON, and a body can only be read once.

suggested.rationale: Calling fetch against real success and error responses in a JavaScript lab is the fastest way to see that a 404 still resolves and to practise checking ok before parsing JSON.

lessons.plain: A template literal is a way of writing text in JavaScript where you can drop values straight into the sentence instead of gluing pieces together with plus signs. You wrap the text in backticks, the slanted quote key, and put any value inside a dollar sign and curly braces. It can also span several lines exactly as typed. Think of a fill-in-the-blanks form letter: the wording is fixed and the blanks fill themselves in. A tagged template goes one step further. It hands the fixed wording and the blank values to a function you write first, so that function can check, clean or reshape them before the final text is built.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a variable named city holds "Lisbon", what do you think JavaScript prints for the text `Welcome to ${city}!` written between backticks, and what would it print if you used ordinary single quotes instead?
lessons.teach:
A template literal is a string written between backticks (`) instead of single or double quotes. Inside it, a placeholder written as ${expression} is replaced by the value of that expression. An expression is any piece of code that produces a value, so ${price * 2} or ${user.name} both work. Template literals also keep line breaks exactly as typed, so multi-line text needs no \n escape characters. This replaces string concatenation, which means joining strings with the + operator, as in 'Hi ' + name + '!'. Concatenation is easy to break with a missing space or quote, and templates read like the final output.

A tagged template is a template literal placed directly after a function name, with no parentheses, like safe`Hi ${name}`. That function is called the tag. JavaScript does not build the string itself; it calls the tag with two kinds of input: an array of the fixed text pieces, and then each placeholder value as a separate argument. The tag returns whatever it wants, usually a finished string.

Worked example: function tag(strings, ...values). The ...values part is a rest parameter, which gathers all remaining arguments into one array. Call tag`Hi ${name}, you have ${n} jobs` with name = "Ana" and n = 3. Step one: strings is ["Hi ", ", you have ", " jobs"]. Step two: values is ["Ana", 3]. Step three: notice strings always has one more item than values, because text surrounds every placeholder. Step four: the tag can loop, joining strings[i] with a cleaned values[i], and return the result.

A common mistake is writing ${name} inside single or double quotes. Nothing is substituted; the literal characters ${name} appear in the output. Only backticks activate placeholders.

In a running system, plain templates insert values unchanged. If user input goes into HTML this way, a user can inject a script tag. A tagged template that escapes each value before joining is a common defence against that.

questions.prompt: A warehouse team at Northbay Logistics writes a tag function, label(strings, ...values), and calls it like this: label`Crate ${id} holds ${count} units for ${dept}.` with id = 58, count = 40 and dept = "Bakery". Trace what the tag receives. Step one: strings is ____. Step two: values is [58, 40, "Bakery"]. Step three: check that strings has one more item than values (4 versus 3), because fixed text surrounds every placeholder. Step four: the tag loops, joining each strings[i] with values[i], adds the last text piece, and returns the finished label. What belongs in the blank in step one?
choices: ["Crate ", " holds ", " units for "]
["Crate ", 58, " holds ", 40, " units for ", "Bakery", "."]
["Crate ", " holds ", " units for ", "."]
["Crate 58 holds 40 units for Bakery."]
questions.why: The strings array holds only the fixed text pieces around the placeholders, including the final ".", so it has four items, one more than the three values.

questions.prompt: At Pinecrest Clinic, a developer writes const line = 'Total: ${sum}'; with sum equal to 12, using ordinary single quotes. What does line contain?
choices: Nothing, because JavaScript throws an error on ${ inside quotes
Total: 12, because ${sum} is replaced wherever it appears
The literal characters Total: ${sum}, because placeholders only work inside backticks
Total: undefined, because quotes hide the variable from the expression
questions.why: Only backticks activate placeholders; inside single or double quotes, ${sum} is just ordinary text and is printed as-is.

questions.prompt: A mailing script at Harbor Credit Union builds a greeting with string concatenation: 'Dear ' + first + ' ' + last + ','. With first = "Lee" and last = "Moss" it produces Dear Lee Moss, . Which template literal produces exactly the same text?
choices: `Dear ${first}${last},`
`Dear ${first} ${last},`
'Dear ${first} ${last},'
`Dear + ${first} + ${last},`
questions.why: Inside backticks, each ${...} is replaced by its value and the spaces and comma are kept exactly as typed, giving Dear Lee Moss, just like the concatenation.

questions.prompt:
A review site for Copperleaf Books builds HTML with a plain template literal: `

${reviewText}

`, where reviewText comes straight from what a visitor typed. What is the risk, and what defence does the idea of tagged templates offer?
choices: The risk is a missing line break; using \n inside the backticks fixes it
The placeholder is ignored in HTML; switching to + concatenation makes the value appear
Tagged templates run the visitor's text as code, so plain templates are the safer choice
A visitor can inject a script tag; a tag function that escapes each value before joining helps prevent it
questions.why: Plain templates insert values unchanged, so typed HTML such as a script tag lands in the page; a tag that cleans each value before joining blocks that.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who still writes 'Hello ' + name + '!' what template literals and tagged templates are, how a tag function receives its inputs, and name one limit or risk of plain template literals.
lessons.modelAnswer: A template literal is a string in backticks where ${...} placeholders are replaced by the value of whatever expression is inside, and line breaks are kept as written. It replaces chains of + concatenation, so it is easier to read and harder to get spacing or quotes wrong. A tagged template puts a function name right before the backticks. Instead of building the string, JavaScript calls that function with an array of the fixed text pieces plus each placeholder value as its own argument; there is always one more text piece than values. The function decides what to return. The risk with plain template literals is that they insert values exactly as they are, so untrusted user input dropped into HTML can inject markup or scripts. A tag that escapes each value first solves that, at the cost of writing and maintaining the tag. Also, placeholders only work inside backticks, not regular quotes.
rubricPoints: Template literals use backticks and ${expression} placeholders that are replaced by values.
They support multi-line text and replace error-prone + concatenation.
A tagged template calls a function placed before the backticks instead of building the string directly.
The tag receives an array of fixed text pieces and the placeholder values separately, with one more text piece than values.
Plain templates insert values unescaped, so untrusted input can cause injection; a tag can sanitize.
Placeholders do nothing inside single or double quotes.

suggested.rationale: Writing a tag function and watching exactly what strings and values arrays it receives is best learned by running code in the planned JavaScript lab.

lessons.plain: An ES module is a JavaScript file that keeps its variables private unless it deliberately shares them. To share something, the file exports it, which is like putting it on a shelf by the shop door. Another file imports it, which is like taking it off that shelf by name. There are two kinds of shelf spot. Named exports carry a label, and the importer must ask for that exact label. A default export is the one main item, and the importer can call it whatever they like. Because files only share what they choose to, they stop accidentally overwriting each other's global variables.
lessons.guessPrompt: If two separate script files both create a variable called total at the top level and are loaded on the same web page, what do you think happens to the first file's total, and how might you stop that?
lessons.teach:
An ES module (ECMAScript module, the standard JavaScript module system) is a file with its own private top-level scope. Scope means the region where a name is visible. Nothing inside a module leaks out unless you export it, and nothing from another module is visible unless you import it. This is why modules replace global variables: two files can both declare total without clashing.

A named export shares a value under its own name, for example export const TAX = 0.2; or export function addTax(x) {...}. A module can have many named exports. You import them with curly braces and the exact same names: import { TAX, addTax } from './tax.js'; You may rename with as, for example import { addTax as withTax }.

A default export marks the single main thing a module provides: export default function formatPrice(n) {...}. A module may have at most one. You import it without braces and choose any local name: import formatPrice from './format.js'; One import line can take both kinds: import formatPrice, { CURRENCY } from './format.js';

Worked example. tax.js contains export const TAX = 0.2; and export function addTax(x) { return x * (1 + TAX); }. main.js contains import { addTax } from './tax.js'; and then console.log(addTax(100));. Step 1: the runtime loads main.js and sees the import. Step 2: it loads tax.js and builds its exports, TAX and addTax. Step 3: it binds the local name addTax to the exported function. Step 4: addTax(100) runs, reads TAX from inside tax.js, and prints 120. main.js never sees TAX, because it did not import it.

A common mistake is mixing up the brace rules. If you write import { formatPrice } from './format.js' when formatPrice is a default export, the import fails with an error saying there is no export with that name. If you drop the braces for a named export, you ask for a default that may not exist.

In a browser, the script tag must say type="module", otherwise import statements cause a syntax error and the page logic never runs. Import paths in browsers also need the file extension, such as .js.

questions.prompt: A bakery website has a file orders.js containing export default function placeOrder(item) { ... } and export const MAX_ITEMS = 12;. A second file, app.js, needs to call placeOrder('bagel') and also check MAX_ITEMS. Step 1: placeOrder is the default export, so it is imported without curly braces and could be given any local name. Step 2: MAX_ITEMS is a named export, so it must go inside curly braces with its exact name. Step 3: (missing) write the single import line at the top of app.js. Step 4: in the HTML page, load app.js with a script tag that says type="module". Which line correctly completes Step 3?
choices: import { placeOrder, MAX_ITEMS } from './orders.js';
import placeOrder, { maxItems } from './orders';
import placeOrder, { MAX_ITEMS } from './orders.js';
import placeOrder, MAX_ITEMS from './orders.js';
questions.why: The default export is imported without braces, the named export goes inside braces with its exact name, and the browser path keeps the .js extension, which together is what this line does.

questions.prompt: A team splits a library app into two ES modules, books.js and members.js. Each file declares let count = 0; at its top level, and neither file exports count. What happens when both modules are loaded on the same page?
choices: Only the module that loads first gets a count variable
The second declaration overwrites the first, so both files share one count
Nothing clashes, because each module has its own private top-level scope
The page throws an error because count is declared twice
questions.why: Each ES module has its own private top-level scope, so names that are not exported stay inside their own file and cannot collide with each other.

questions.prompt: cart.js contains export default class Cart { ... } and nothing else. In checkout.js a developer writes import ShoppingCart from './cart.js'; and then uses new ShoppingCart(). What is the result?
choices: It fails, because default imports need curly braces
It fails, because a class cannot be a default export
It fails, because the local name must exactly match the class name Cart
It works, because a default import can use any local name you choose
questions.why: A default export is imported without braces, and the importing file may choose any local name for it, so ShoppingCart refers to the Cart class.

questions.prompt: A weather dashboard's HTML loads its main file with <script src="dashboard.js"></script>. The first line of dashboard.js is import { getForecast } from './forecast.js';. What happens in the browser?
choices: The browser loads forecast.js automatically and the page works
Only getForecast is skipped, and the rest of dashboard.js runs normally
The browser treats getForecast as a global variable instead
The import causes a syntax error and the dashboard logic never runs
questions.why: Without type="module" on the script tag, the browser does not treat the file as a module, so the import statement is a syntax error and none of the script runs.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between default and named exports, when you would choose each, and one tradeoff or pitfall of default exports.
lessons.modelAnswer: An ES module keeps everything private unless it exports it, so files stop fighting over global names. Named exports share values under fixed names. A file can have many of them, and importers use curly braces with those exact names, renaming with as if they need to. A default export is the one main thing a file provides. There is only one per file, and the importer picks any name without braces. I would use named exports for a utility file with several helpers, and a default export when a file really has one main job, like a single component or class. The tradeoff is that default imports can be named anything. Different files may call the same thing by different names, which makes searching and refactoring harder, and editors cannot catch a mistyped name the way they can with named imports. Mixing up the brace rules is the most common import error.
rubricPoints: Modules have private scope, and only exported items are visible to other files.
Named exports can be many per file and are imported with braces using the exact name, or renamed with as.
A file has at most one default export, imported without braces under any chosen name.
Mixing up the brace rules causes import errors.
Default exports can be imported under inconsistent names, which hurts searching, refactoring and tooling.
In the browser, scripts must load with type="module".

suggested.rationale: Splitting a script into modules and fixing broken import and export lines is best learned by running real files, which a planned JavaScript lab would allow and no current mission covers.

lessons.plain: A class in JavaScript is a blueprint for making many objects that share the same shape and behaviour. Think of a cookie cutter: the cutter is the class, and each cookie is an object made from it. The constructor is the setup step that runs whenever you make a new object, filling in that object's own details. Methods are actions that every object made from the class can perform. Inheritance lets one class build on another, like a fancy cutter that starts from the plain one and adds icing. Static members belong to the cutter itself, not to any single cookie.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose you have a basic Vehicle blueprint and want a Truck blueprint that can do everything a Vehicle does, plus carry a load. Where would you write the shared behaviour so you only write it once, and how might Truck reuse it?
lessons.teach:
A class is a template for creating objects. You create an object from it with the keyword new, and that object is called an instance. The constructor is a special function inside the class that runs once per new instance. Inside it, the word this means the instance being built, so this.id = id stores data on that one object. A method is a function defined in the class body. JavaScript keeps methods on the class's shared prototype, which is a hidden object that all instances look up to. That means methods are shared rather than copied, which saves memory. Inheritance means one class extends another: class Truck extends Vehicle. The child class gets the parent's methods. Inside the child, super(...) calls the parent's constructor, and super.method() calls the parent's version of a method. A static member is marked with the keyword static. It belongs to the class itself, so you use it as Vehicle.count, not through an instance.

Worked example. Vehicle has static count = 0. Its constructor(id) sets this.id = id and adds 1 to Vehicle.count. Its describe() method returns "Vehicle " + this.id. Truck extends Vehicle. Its constructor(id, load) calls super(id), then sets this.load = load. Truck's describe() returns super.describe() + " carrying " + this.load + " kg". Now trace new Truck("T1", 500). First, Truck's constructor starts. Next, super("T1") runs Vehicle's constructor, which sets id to "T1" and raises Vehicle.count to 1. Then load is set to 500. Calling describe() finds Truck's own version first. That version calls the parent's describe, which gives "Vehicle T1", and then appends the load, producing "Vehicle T1 carrying 500 kg". Vehicle.count is 1, but asking the instance for count gives undefined.

A common mistake is using this in a child constructor before calling super(). JavaScript throws a ReferenceError at the moment the object is created. In a running program, that means every attempt to build that kind of object crashes.

questions.prompt:
A library app has a parent class Book and a child class EBook.

Book has static created, which is currently 3 because three books already exist. Book's constructor(title) sets this.title = title and adds 1 to Book.created. Book's label() method returns "Book: " + this.title.

EBook extends Book. Its constructor(title, sizeMb) calls super(title), then sets this.sizeMb = sizeMb. EBook's label() returns super.label() + " (" + this.sizeMb + " MB)".

Trace new EBook("Dune", 12).
Step 1: EBook's constructor starts.
Step 2: ???
Step 3: sizeMb is set to 12 on the new instance.
Step 4: Calling label() finds EBook's own version first. It calls the parent's label, which gives "Book: Dune", then appends the size, producing "Book: Dune (12 MB)".

Which choice correctly fills in Step 2?
choices: this.sizeMb is stored first, and Book's constructor is then called automatically after EBook's finishes
super("Dune") copies Book's label method onto the new object as a private copy and resets Book.created back to 1
super("Dune") runs EBook's own constructor a second time, which sets title but leaves Book.created at 3
super("Dune") runs Book's constructor, which sets title to "Dune" and raises Book.created from 3 to 4
questions.why: super(...) inside a child constructor calls the parent's constructor, so Book's code runs for this instance: it stores the title and adds 1 to the static counter, taking it from 3 to 4.

questions.prompt: A weather station program defines class Sensor with the line static unit = "celsius". It then creates an instance with const s = new Sensor(). What do Sensor.unit and s.unit give?
choices: Sensor.unit gives "celsius"; s.unit gives undefined
Sensor.unit gives undefined; s.unit gives "celsius"
Both give undefined until the constructor sets this.unit
Both give "celsius", because instances inherit everything in the class
questions.why: A static member belongs to the class itself, so you read it through the class name; asking an instance for it gives undefined.

questions.prompt: A payroll team writes class Manager extends Employee. Manager's constructor(name, team) first runs this.team = team and only then calls super(name). What happens when the program runs new Manager("Ana", "Ops")?
choices: team is stored, but name is silently skipped and left as undefined
A ReferenceError is thrown as the object is created, so every attempt to build a Manager crashes
Employee's constructor runs twice, once automatically and once from super(name)
The object is built normally, because the order of lines in a constructor does not matter
questions.why: Using this in a child constructor before calling super() throws a ReferenceError at creation time, so no Manager can ever be built until the order is fixed.

questions.prompt: An online shop creates 10,000 instances of class Order, and Order has one method, total(), defined in the class body. How many copies of the total function does JavaScript keep?
choices: One per call, created fresh every time total() runs
One, kept on the class's shared prototype that all instances look up to
10,000, one stored inside each Order instance
Zero until total() is marked static, then exactly one
questions.why: Methods defined in a class body live on the shared prototype, so all instances use the same single function instead of each holding a copy, which saves memory.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a JavaScript class uses a constructor, methods, inheritance with extends and super, and static members. Name one limit or tradeoff of relying on inheritance or static members.
lessons.modelAnswer: A class is a blueprint, and new builds an instance from it. The constructor runs once per instance and uses this to store that object's own data. Methods live on a shared prototype, so every instance uses one copy of each method instead of carrying its own. With extends, a child class inherits the parent's methods. In the child's constructor, I have to call super() before touching this, or I get a ReferenceError. I can also override a method and still reach the parent's version with super.method(). Static members belong to the class itself, like Vehicle.count, so I can't reach them through an instance. One tradeoff is that inheritance ties the child tightly to the parent. If I change the parent, every subclass can break, and deep chains get hard to follow. Static fields also act like shared global state for that class, so any code can change them.
rubricPoints: The constructor runs once per new instance and sets that instance's data through this.
Methods are defined once on the class and shared by all instances through the prototype.
extends gives a child class the parent's methods, and super() must be called before this in the child constructor.
super.method() lets an overriding method reuse the parent's version.
Static members belong to the class itself and are not reachable from instances.
Names a tradeoff, such as tight coupling in inheritance chains or static fields acting as shared state.

suggested.rationale: Learners understand classes best by writing a parent and child class, running them, and watching super(), overriding and static lookups behave, which the planned JavaScript lab would let them do.

lessons.plain: Map and Set are two built-in JavaScript collections added in the ES6 update to the language. A Map is a lookup table: you store a value under a key and fetch it back by that key, and the key can be any kind of value, not just text. A Set is a bag that keeps each value only once, so duplicates are silently dropped. Think of a Map as a coat check, where the ticket gets your coat back, and a Set as a guest list, where writing a name twice still means one guest.
lessons.guessPrompt: You have the list of tags ['js', 'web', 'js', 'node', 'web']. If you put them into a collection that refuses to keep duplicates, how many items would it hold, and which ones?
lessons.teach:
A Map is a key-value collection. A key is the label you look something up by, and a value is what is stored under it. Its main methods are set(key, value), get(key), has(key) and delete(key), and its size property gives the count. A Set is a collection of unique values, with add(value), has(value), delete(value) and size. Both remember insertion order, the order items were first added, and both can be looped with for...of.

Why use them instead of plain objects and arrays? A plain object converts every key to a string, so the number 1 and the text '1' collide, and an object or element cannot serve as a real key. An object also inherits built-in names such as 'constructor' from its prototype (the shared parent object it borrows properties from), which can clash with your data, and it has no size property. An array allows duplicates, and checking membership with includes scans every element, which slows down as the array grows. Set.has and Map.get use hashing, so lookups stay fast regardless of size.

Worked example, counting page visits. Start with const visits = new Map(). A visit to '/home' arrives: visits.get('/home') is undefined, so we call visits.set('/home', 1). Another '/home' visit: get returns 1, so we set it to 2. A '/about' visit sets '/about' to 1. Now visits.size is 2 and visits.get('/home') is 2. For unique tags, new Set(['js', 'web', 'js']) holds 'js' and 'web', size 2, and [...set] turns it back into an array.

Common mistake: writing visits['/home'] = 1 on a Map. That attaches an ordinary property to the Map object instead of creating an entry, so get, has and size never see it. A second trap: Sets compare objects by identity, so two separate objects with identical contents both stay. In a running app these bugs show up as counts that never change, lookups that miss, or lists that still contain duplicates.

questions.prompt: A small cinema uses a Set to stop a seat being sold twice. It starts with const booked = new Set(). Step 1: a request for seat 'C4' arrives. booked.has('C4') is false, so the code calls booked.add('C4'). Step 2: a request for 'D1' arrives. booked.has('D1') is false, so booked.add('D1') runs and booked.size is now 2. Step 3: another request for 'C4' arrives. What correctly happens at step 3?
choices: booked.has('C4') is false, so 'C4' is added again and booked.size becomes 3
booked.add('C4') throws an error because 'C4' is already in the Set
booked.has('C4') is true, so the booking is refused and booked.size stays 2
booked.has('C4') is true, and add replaces the old 'C4', moving it to the end of the order
questions.why: 'C4' was added in step 1, so has returns true, and a Set never stores a value twice, so the size stays 2.

questions.prompt: A warehouse script runs const bins = new Map(); bins.set(7, 'bolts'); bins.set('7', 'nuts'); What is bins.size, and why?
choices: 1, because a Map turns every key into a string, just as a plain object does
2, because a Map allows duplicate keys as long as their values differ
1, because the second set overwrites the first, since both keys become '7'
2, because a Map keeps the number 7 and the text '7' as separate keys
questions.why: A Map does not convert keys to strings, so 7 and '7' are different keys. A plain object would merge them into one key.

questions.prompt: A forum must check each new post's author against a list of 80,000 banned usernames, and the list keeps growing. Which choice best keeps these checks fast as the list grows?
choices: Store the names in an array and sort it, so includes finishes sooner
Store the names in a Set and call has, because it uses hashing instead of scanning every element
Store the names in an array and call includes, because arrays remember insertion order
Store the names as keys of a plain object, because objects have a size property
questions.why: Set.has uses hashing, so lookups stay fast however large the Set gets. Array includes checks every element, so it slows down as the list grows.

questions.prompt: A bike-rental app runs const stock = new Map(); stock['helmets'] = 12; and then later checks stock.has('helmets') and stock.size. What does it get?
choices: false and 0, because bracket assignment adds an ordinary property, not a Map entry
An error, because a Map refuses bracket assignment
true and 1, because bracket assignment is a shortcut for set
true and 0, because size only counts entries added with add
questions.why: Writing stock['helmets'] attaches a plain property to the Map object. has, get and size only see entries created with set, so has returns false and size stays 0.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would choose a Map or a Set over a plain object or array, and name one limit or tradeoff of using them.
lessons.modelAnswer: I reach for a Map when I need a lookup table whose keys are not plain strings, or whose keys come from user data that might collide with built-in object names like 'constructor'. A Map keeps keys as their real type, remembers insertion order, has a size property, and gives fast get and has. I use a Set when I only care whether something is present and want duplicates removed automatically. Set.has stays fast as the collection grows, unlike array.includes, which scans every element. There are tradeoffs. You must use get and set, because bracket assignment on a Map adds a property, not an entry. Sets and Maps compare objects by identity, so two lookalike objects count as different. Also, JSON.stringify does not serialize a Map's entries, so you have to convert to an array or object before sending it as JSON.
rubricPoints: Map stores key-value pairs where keys keep their real type, including objects.
Set stores only unique values and drops duplicates automatically.
Both keep insertion order, have a size property, and offer fast has lookups compared with scanning an array.
Plain objects coerce keys to strings and can collide with inherited prototype names.
Names a limit, such as bracket syntax not working, identity comparison of objects, or no direct JSON serialization.

suggested.rationale: Choosing between Map, Set, objects and arrays sticks best by running small JavaScript snippets and watching duplicates, key types and sizes behave, which a JavaScript lab would provide.

lessons.plain: Optional chaining and nullish coalescing are two short JavaScript operators for handling missing data safely. Optional chaining, written ?., lets you reach into nested data and quietly get undefined if a step along the way is missing, instead of crashing. Nullish coalescing, written ??, supplies a fallback value only when something is truly missing (null or undefined), not when it is a legitimate zero or empty text. Picture asking a receptionist to pass a note to someone's assistant: if there is no assistant, the receptionist just says nobody is there instead of panicking, and you then decide on a sensible default.
lessons.guessPrompt: A settings object stores a user's volume as 0, meaning muted. If you write 'volume || 50' to fill in a default when the volume is missing, what value do you think you get, and is that what the user wanted?
lessons.teach:
Optional chaining (?.) reads a property, element, or method only if the value on its left is not nullish. Nullish means exactly null (deliberately empty) or undefined (never set). If the left side is nullish, the whole expression stops immediately and returns undefined. Stopping early like this is called short-circuiting. Without it, reading a property of undefined throws a TypeError, an error that halts the running code. Nullish coalescing (??) returns its right side only when its left side is nullish; otherwise it returns the left side unchanged.

This matters because of falsy values, the values JavaScript treats as false in a condition: false, 0, empty string '', NaN, null and undefined. The older logical OR operator (||) falls back on any falsy value, so it wrongly replaces real data like 0 or ''.

Worked example. Take const user = { settings: { volume: 0 } }. First, user.profile?.name: user.profile is undefined, so ?. short-circuits and the result is undefined, with no crash. Second, user.settings?.volume: settings exists, so we read volume and get 0. Third, user.settings?.volume ?? 50: the left side is 0, which is not nullish, so the result stays 0. Fourth, compare user.settings?.volume || 50: 0 is falsy, so OR returns 50, and the muted user suddenly gets loud audio. You can also call methods safely with obj.method?.() and index safely with arr?.[0].

Common mistake: using || for defaults when 0, false or '' are valid values, which silently overwrites real data. A second mistake is sprinkling ?. everywhere, including on data that must always exist; that hides bugs by turning a loud crash into a quiet undefined that surfaces far away.

In a running system, a missing ?. on optional API data can crash a page render, while a misplaced || can save wrong settings without any error at all.

questions.prompt:
A bakery app stores const order = { customer: null, discount: 0, note: '' }. Trace each expression.
Step 1: order.customer?.email. customer is null, which is nullish, so ?. short-circuits and the result is undefined. Nothing crashes.
Step 2: order.discount ?? 10. The left side is 0. 0 is not nullish, so ?? keeps it and the result is 0.
Step 3: order.coupon ?? 'NONE'. coupon was never set, so it is undefined. That is nullish, so the result is 'NONE'.
Step 4: order.note ?? 'No note'. What is the result, and why?
choices: '' (the empty string), because '' is not nullish, so ?? keeps the left side
A TypeError, because note holds no text and cannot be read
undefined, because ?? treats an empty string as missing
'No note', because an empty string is falsy and ?? replaces falsy values
questions.why: ?? falls back only on null or undefined. An empty string is falsy but not nullish, so ?? returns '' unchanged.

questions.prompt: Which values on the left side make the nullish coalescing operator (??) return its right side?
choices: Any falsy value, such as 0, '', false or NaN
Only null or undefined
Only undefined; null counts as a real value
Any value that is not a number or a string
questions.why: Nullish means exactly null or undefined, and ?? falls back only on those two values.

questions.prompt: A game stores const player = { lives: 0 }. The screen shows the value of player.lives || 3. What appears, and why?
choices: undefined, because a property holding 0 counts as missing
0, because || only replaces null and undefined, and lives is set
3, because 0 is falsy, so || falls back to the right side
A TypeError, because 0 cannot be combined with ||
questions.why: Logical OR falls back on any falsy value, so the real value 0 is overwritten with 3. Using ?? would keep the 0.

questions.prompt: In an invoicing tool, every invoice must always have an id. A developer writes invoice?.id everywhere just to be safe. One day a bug passes undefined in place of an invoice. What is the most likely effect?
choices: The id is automatically replaced with a default value.
?. turns the undefined invoice into an empty object, so everything works correctly.
No crash at that line. An undefined id travels on quietly and causes a confusing problem somewhere else.
A TypeError at that line, which points straight to the bug.
questions.why: Overusing ?. on data that must exist hides bugs. It turns a loud crash into a quiet undefined that shows up far from the real cause.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what ?. and ?? do, why ?? is often safer than || for default values, and name one situation where using optional chaining would be a bad idea.
lessons.modelAnswer: Optional chaining, ?., lets me read nested data without crashing. If the thing on the left is null or undefined, the expression stops and gives undefined instead of throwing a TypeError. So order.customer?.address?.city is safe even if a customer has no address. Nullish coalescing, ??, gives a fallback only when the left side is null or undefined. That makes it safer than || for defaults, because || also replaces 0, false and empty strings. If a discount is 0, discount || 10 wrongly returns 10, but discount ?? 10 keeps 0. The tradeoff is that ?. can hide real bugs. If a value must always be present, like the logged-in user's ID after login, writing user?.id turns a clear crash into a silent undefined that causes confusing failures later. I'd use ?. only where data is genuinely optional.
rubricPoints: Optional chaining returns undefined instead of throwing when a step is null or undefined.
Nullish coalescing falls back only on null or undefined.
Logical OR falls back on any falsy value such as 0, false or empty string, which can overwrite valid data.
Gives a concrete example where ?? and || produce different results.
Names the tradeoff that overusing ?. can hide bugs on data that should always exist.

suggested.rationale: Running small snippets and watching ?? and || diverge on values like 0, or ?. prevent a TypeError, builds the intuition faster than reading alone.

lessons.plain: Every JavaScript object carries a hidden link to another object, called its prototype. When you ask an object for a property or method it does not have, JavaScript quietly follows that link and asks the prototype, then the prototype's prototype, and so on. This series of links is the prototype chain. Think of asking a junior colleague a question: if they don't know, they ask their manager, who asks their director, until someone answers or the top of the company admits nobody knows. Methods like those every list or text value has are not copied into each value; they live once on a shared prototype and are found by this upward search.
lessons.guessPrompt: You create an empty list with [] and call a method on it that you never wrote, such as toString. The list itself contains no items and no functions you added. Where do you think JavaScript finds that method?
lessons.teach:
The prototype chain is the sequence of linked objects JavaScript searches when you read a property. A prototype is an ordinary object that another object points to through a hidden internal link, often written [[Prototype]]. An own property is one stored directly on the object itself. Lookup works like this: check the object's own properties; if the name is missing, follow the link to its prototype and check there; repeat. The chain ends at Object.prototype, the base object most chains share, whose own link is null (meaning no further object). If the search reaches null without a match, the read returns undefined.

This works because behaviour can live in one shared place. Thousands of arrays share a single copy of push, saving memory and letting one change reach every array.

Worked example: const arr = [1, 2]. Calling arr.push(3): step 1, arr has own properties 0, 1 and length, but no push. Step 2, follow the link to Array.prototype, which owns push. Found; it runs. Calling arr.hasOwnProperty('length'): arr lacks it, Array.prototype lacks it, Object.prototype owns it. Found two steps up. Reading arr.fly: not on arr, Array.prototype or Object.prototype, then null, so the result is undefined, and calling arr.fly() throws a TypeError saying it is not a function. Wherever a method is found, inside it this still means arr, the object you called it on.

A common mistake is thinking that assigning to an inherited name changes the prototype. Writing arr.push = something creates a new own property on arr that shadows (hides) the shared one; other arrays are unaffected. The reverse is the real danger in a running system: adding or changing a property on a shared prototype instantly changes behaviour for every object linked to it, which can break unrelated code. Reads walk the chain; ordinary writes land on the object itself.

questions.prompt: A library app has an object named loan with own properties bookId and dueDate. Its prototype is an object named loanTools, which owns a method renew. The prototype of loanTools is Object.prototype. The code calls loan.toString(). Trace the lookup. Step 1: loan's own properties are bookId and dueDate, with no toString, so follow the link. Step 2: loanTools owns renew but not toString, so follow the link again. Step 3: ______. Which choice correctly completes step 3?
choices: Object.prototype is not checked because the search stops after the first prototype, so the read returns undefined.
Object.prototype owns toString, so it is found two steps up and runs, and inside it this means loan.
Object.prototype is reached, but because toString was not on loan or loanTools, the call throws a TypeError.
Object.prototype owns toString, so it runs, and inside it this means Object.prototype because that is where it was found.
questions.why: The search keeps following links until a match or null, and Object.prototype owns toString, but this still refers to the object the method was called on, which is loan.

questions.prompt: A weather service has an object named sensor with one own property, reading. Its prototype is deviceBase, which owns a method reset. The prototype of deviceBase is Object.prototype, whose own link is null. No object in this chain has a property named calibrate. What does reading sensor.calibrate (without calling it) give?
choices: undefined
A TypeError saying calibrate is not a function
The deviceBase object, because it is the nearest prototype
null, because the chain ends at null
questions.why: The search checks sensor, deviceBase and Object.prototype, reaches null with no match, and a read that finds nothing returns undefined. Only calling it would throw a TypeError.

questions.prompt: In a billing system, two objects, invoiceA and invoiceB, have the same prototype, invoiceProto, which owns a method format. Neither invoice has its own format. The code runs invoiceA.format = customFormatter. Afterwards, what happens when each invoice's format is read?
choices: invoiceB now uses customFormatter, and invoiceA keeps the shared format.
invoiceA gets its own format that shadows the shared one, and invoiceB still finds the original format on invoiceProto.
invoiceProto.format is replaced, so both invoices now use customFormatter.
The assignment fails silently because format is inherited, so both invoices keep using the shared format.
questions.why: An ordinary write lands on the object itself, creating an own property on invoiceA that hides the inherited one. The prototype and invoiceB are untouched.

questions.prompt: A support-ticket service has 5,000 ticket objects that all link to one prototype, ticketProto, which owns a method close. None of the tickets has its own close. To fix one ticket, a developer edits ticketProto.close directly and accidentally introduces a bug. What is the effect on the running service?
choices: Only the ticket the developer was fixing is affected, because each ticket keeps its own copy of close.
All 5,000 tickets immediately use the buggy close, because they all find close on the shared prototype.
Every ticket stops finding close, so calling it throws a TypeError.
No ticket is affected until each one is recreated, because tickets copy their prototype's methods when they are made.
questions.why: Behaviour on a shared prototype exists in one place, so changing it instantly changes what every linked object finds during lookup. That can break code far from the original fix.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, what happens step by step when code calls a method on an object that does not define that method itself, and name one risk or tradeoff of sharing behaviour this way.
lessons.modelAnswer: Each object has a hidden link to a prototype object. When I call obj.method(), JavaScript first looks at obj's own properties. If the name isn't there, it follows the link to the prototype and looks again, then that object's prototype, until it finds the name or reaches the end of the chain, which is null. Most chains end at Object.prototype before null. If nothing matches, reading gives undefined and calling it throws a 'not a function' TypeError. When a method is found higher up, this still refers to obj, the original object. The benefit is that one copy of a method serves every linked object. The tradeoff is shared blast radius: changing a prototype changes every object linked to it, possibly breaking unrelated code. Also, assigning a same-named property on obj only shadows the inherited one for obj; it doesn't change the prototype.
rubricPoints: Every object has a hidden link to a prototype object.
Lookup checks own properties first, then walks up the chain one prototype at a time.
The chain ends at null, usually after Object.prototype, and a missing property reads as undefined.
Inside an inherited method, this still refers to the object the method was called on.
Assigning a property creates an own property that shadows the inherited one rather than changing the prototype.
Names a tradeoff, such as changes to a shared prototype affecting every linked object.

suggested.rationale: Predicting a property lookup and then running it to check where it was found is best learned by hands-on experiments in a JavaScript lab.

lessons.plain: In JavaScript, objects can borrow behaviour directly from other objects. Object.create makes a brand-new, empty object and quietly links it to an existing object you choose, called its prototype. When you ask the new object for something it does not have, JavaScript checks the linked object instead. That is prototypal inheritance: objects inheriting from objects. Classical inheritance, found in languages like Java, works differently: you first write a class, a blueprint, and objects are stamped out from it. Think of prototypal inheritance as asking a knowledgeable colleague when you don't know something, rather than being built from a factory mould.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you make a new object linked to an existing 'animal' object that has a speak method, and the new object has no speak method of its own, what do you think happens when you call speak on the new object?
lessons.teach:
Object.create(proto) is a built-in function that returns a new, empty object whose prototype is proto. A prototype is simply another object that JavaScript consults when a property is missing. Prototypal inheritance means objects inherit directly from other live objects. Classical inheritance means objects get their behaviour from a class, a blueprint that is defined separately and from which instances are made; subclasses extend parent classes.

Why it works: every JavaScript object carries a hidden link to its prototype. A property lookup first checks the object itself; if the property is absent, it follows the link. Object.create lets you set that link explicitly, with no class or constructor function required.

Worked example. Let animal = { sound: 'generic noise', speak() { return this.sound; } }. Then let dog = Object.create(animal). Step 1: dog is empty, and its prototype is animal. Step 2: dog.speak() is called; dog has no speak, so JavaScript finds speak on animal. Step 3: inside speak, this refers to dog, the object the method was called on. Step 4: this.sound is looked up on dog, not found, so animal's 'generic noise' is returned. Step 5: set dog.sound = 'woof'. Now dog.speak() returns 'woof', because the own property is found first and shadows, meaning hides, the inherited one.

JavaScript's class keyword looks classical, but underneath it still builds prototype links; it is mostly a tidier syntax over the same mechanism.

Common mistake: assuming Object.create copies the prototype's properties. It does not copy anything; it links. So if you later change animal.sound, every object linked to animal that lacks its own sound sees the change. In a running program, putting a shared mutable value such as an array on a prototype means one object pushing into it silently alters data for all the others, a confusing bug. Keep shared methods on the prototype and per-object data on each object.

questions.prompt:
A ticketing app shares display settings through a prototype. Let config = { theme: 'light', label() { return 'Theme: ' + this.theme; } }. Then let userA = Object.create(config) and let userB = Object.create(config).

Step 1: userA and userB are both empty, and each has config as its prototype.
Step 2: userA.theme = 'dark' is run, giving userA its own theme property.
Step 3: config.theme = 'blue' is run, changing the prototype object itself.
Step 4: userB.label() is called. userB has no label, so JavaScript finds label on config, and inside it this refers to userB.
Step 5: ???
Step 6: userA.label() returns 'Theme: dark', because userA's own theme is found first and shadows the inherited one.

Which choice correctly fills in Step 5?
choices: this.theme is looked up on userB and not found, so JavaScript throws an error, because a missing own property cannot be read through a prototype.
this.theme is looked up on userB, and because userA set theme to 'dark' on the shared prototype, the result is 'Theme: dark'.
this.theme is looked up on userB, which got its own copy of theme ('light') when Object.create ran, so the result is 'Theme: light'.
this.theme is looked up on userB, not found, so the lookup follows the link to config, which now holds 'blue', giving 'Theme: blue'.
questions.why: Object.create links rather than copies, so userB, lacking its own theme, sees config's current value 'blue', while userA's assignment created an own property on userA only.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes the difference between prototypal inheritance and classical inheritance?
choices: In prototypal inheritance an object inherits directly from another live object; in classical inheritance instances get behaviour from a separately defined class blueprint.
Prototypal inheritance requires a constructor function to set the link; classical inheritance lets you link any two objects with no blueprint.
Prototypal inheritance only works for methods, while classical inheritance is the only way to inherit data properties such as strings or numbers.
In prototypal inheritance an object receives a full copy of another object's properties; in classical inheritance objects share one live object.
questions.why: Prototypal inheritance links objects to other existing objects, whereas classical inheritance makes instances from a class blueprint that subclasses can extend.

questions.prompt: A sports club app defines team = { members: [], add(name) { this.members.push(name); } }. It then creates squadA = Object.create(team) and squadB = Object.create(team), and runs squadA.add('Rui'). What is squadB.members.length?
choices: An error is thrown, because push cannot be called through a prototype
1, because both squads reach the same members array on team, and push changed it
undefined, because squadB has no members property of its own
0, because Object.create gave squadB its own separate empty members array
questions.why: Neither squad has its own members, so this.members resolves to the single array on team, and pushing into it changes the data every linked object sees.

questions.prompt: A developer says: "Because I used the class keyword, my JavaScript objects use true classical inheritance and no prototype links are involved." What is the most accurate response?
choices: Correct: the class keyword switches JavaScript to a separate inheritance system that replaces prototypes entirely.
Not quite: class is mostly tidier syntax, and underneath it still builds prototype links that property lookups follow.
Not quite: class copies every parent property onto each instance, so no links exist, but this is still called prototypal.
Correct: prototype links are only created when you call Object.create directly, never in any other way.
questions.why: JavaScript's class keyword looks classical but still works through the same prototype-link mechanism that Object.create sets explicitly.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how Object.create and prototypal inheritance differ from classical, class-based inheritance, and name one limit or tradeoff of the prototypal approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: Object.create makes a new empty object and sets another object as its prototype. If you ask the new object for a property it lacks, JavaScript looks on the prototype. So inheritance is object-to-object, decided at runtime, with no blueprint needed. Classical inheritance, as in Java, defines a class first and creates instances from it, with subclasses extending parents. JavaScript's class keyword is mostly syntax over the same prototype links. The big upside is flexibility: you can link any object to any other and change behaviour on the fly. The tradeoff is that nothing is copied, only linked. If you change the prototype later, or put a mutable array on it, every linked object sees the change, which can cause surprising shared-state bugs. So put shared methods on the prototype and per-object data on each object.
rubricPoints: Object.create returns a new object whose prototype is the object passed in.
Missing properties are looked up on the prototype through a link, not copied.
Classical inheritance builds instances from a class blueprint, while prototypal links objects to objects.
JavaScript's class keyword still uses prototypes underneath.
Names a tradeoff such as shared mutable state on the prototype affecting all linked objects.

suggested.rationale: Creating objects with Object.create and watching lookups and shadowing in a live JavaScript lab makes the link-not-copy behaviour concrete.

lessons.plain: A higher-order function is a function that takes another function as an input, gives back a function as its result, or does both. JavaScript treats functions as ordinary values, like numbers or text, so you can pass them around and store them. Picture a coffee machine that accepts a recipe card. The machine handles the routine work of heating and pouring, and the card you slot in decides which drink comes out. The machine is the higher-order function, and the card is the function you hand it. You write the routine once and swap in only the part that changes.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose you write one loop that doubles every price in a list, then a second loop that adds 10% tax to every price. Which parts of the two loops are identical, and which single part is different?
lessons.teach:
A higher-order function is a function that accepts a function as an argument, returns a function, or both. This works because JavaScript functions are first-class values. That means a function can be stored in a variable, passed into another function, or returned from one, just like a number. A function you pass in to be called later is called a callback.

The benefit is separating the routine from the varying detail. Arrays have built-in higher-order methods. The map method runs a callback on every element and collects the results into a new array. The filter method keeps only the elements for which the callback returns true.

Here is a worked example that takes a function. Run [3, 8, 1].filter(n => n > 2). First, filter calls the callback with 3. The test 3 > 2 is true, so 3 is kept. Next it calls the callback with 8, which is true, so 8 is kept. Then it calls it with 1, which is false, so 1 is dropped. The result is a new array, [3, 8]. You never wrote the loop yourself. You only supplied the rule.

Here is a worked example that returns a function. Write function multiplier(factor) { return n => n * factor; }. Calling multiplier(3) returns a new function that remembers factor = 3. Remembering a variable from the place where a function was created is called a closure. So if you write const triple = multiplier(3), then triple(5) gives 15.

A common mistake is calling a function when you meant to pass it. For example, prices.map(double()) runs double immediately and passes its result, not the function. That usually throws a TypeError or gives wrong values. Similarly, setTimeout(save(), 1000) runs save right away instead of after one second. In a running app, the action then happens at the wrong time, or happens once instead of on every event. Pass the name without parentheses, double or save, so the higher-order function decides when to call it.
